case_strength_assessment:
HONEST VERDICT: Case 002 is the right pick for us ONLY if we build the wardrobe concept (Concept 1). If we were going to build a personalised recommender, Case 001 has strictly better evidence and we should take that instead.

WHY 002 IS STRONG:
1. It is the only case where the AUDIENCE ALSO HAS INVENTORY. Sofia's notebook literally contains the unbuilt product: E-05.3 "let people tell me what they already own" and "maybe the answer is not a shop". Three separate DMs corroborate it (@laura "help me use what I own", @maya_m "I bought the shoes, what should I wear with them", @niamhh "I live in trainers, how would you change it") plus a named persona (E-07.2 Jamie, "owns basics, wants styling help, HIGH REPEAT"). Neither Maya (001) nor Aditi (003) has an equivalent — you cannot bring your own skincare shelf or your own conference access in a way that generates combinatorics. This mechanic is uncopyable by teams on the other cases and produces a visual nobody else will have.
2. The subjective layer in E-04 is richer than 001's. 001 gives numeric ratings (9.2, 8.1) which are already machine-readable and therefore boring. 002 gives pure qualitative judgement with no numbers at all — "great, but warm", "soft but pills", "my actual uniform", "£35 is enough", "best with trainers". Turning THAT into calibrated numbers is exactly what Jev does and nothing else does. The case file even tells you: "the subjective layer is not noise, it is the product."
3. E-06.1 is the sharpest brief line in any of the three cases: "capture how I think about clothes — not just what I own". That single clause authorises a product that judges items Sofia has never seen (Concept 2) and is the cleanest possible commercial story.
4. Her own rule (E-05.1, "if I wouldn't text this to my sister, I don't link it") is IDENTICAL IN SHAPE to the 16:00 finding (E-09.4, 41% of purchases follow a share to a friend). The creator's private decision rule and the audience's highest-value invisible behaviour are the same object. That is a gift and I have not seen it in 001 or 003 as cleanly (003's version, "if I would not say it to my sister on the phone", has no matching share-to-sister DM).

WHERE 002 IS WEAK — DO NOT IGNORE THESE:
1. NO IMAGES. Fashion is the most visual vertical and we have zero product photography, zero look photography, and eight hours. A team that scrapes or mocks pretty product shots will out-WOW a well-reasoned typographic demo in a fashion category. This is the single biggest risk. Mitigation: commit hard to the dossier/surveillance aesthetic — monochrome, mono type, redacted blocks, abstract silhouettes. It matches the heist theme, dodges the image problem, and reads as more premium than everyone else's Pinterest grid. But it IS a mitigation, not a win. Do not attempt to half-do photography; half-done fashion imagery looks worse than none.
2. THIN INVENTORY. E-04 gives 8 of a claimed 36 items. Concepts 1 and 2 need more. We will have to synthesise items in Sofia's voice. Judges may notice. Be explicit on stage: "8 real, the rest extrapolated in her voice" — owning it is stronger than being caught.
3. SIZING IS A TRAP. @hannah (E-01.6, "I'm usually an 8 but brands are all over the place") is bait. Fit prediction is unsolvable in 8 hours and failing it publicly kills trust. Skip fit entirely; if asked, say we deliberately excluded the one question where a wrong answer costs the audience money.
4. TONE MISMATCH RISK. Sofia's asset is warmth ("best-dressed friend"). A cold probability dashboard will read as exactly the "handed to a machine" failure the briefs warn about. The calibration must be dressed as confidence, not as analytics.

VERSUS THE OTHER TWO:
- CASE 001 (Maya, beauty): the richest and most exploitable evidence set of the three — 12 DMs, 6 personas, a 10-item inventory with numeric ratings AND notes, an explicit decision tree in her own handwriting (E-02.2 DRY→Cloud Cream + Barrier Oil), seized physical items with a sticky note that states the thesis ("people do not need more products, they need confidence"), and — uniquely — a DISCOUNTED LEADS sheet (E-08) that pre-kills the wrong answers for you. It is the easiest case to score well on "use of the evidence". It is also, for exactly that reason, THE MOST CROWDED. It is listed first, it is the most literal ("get her out of the reply loop"), and half the room will build a skincare quiz or a DM triage bot. A skincare quiz is a solved genre; it cannot WOW. Pick 001 only if you want a safe mid-table finish.
- CASE 003 (Aditi, tech media): highest-status creator, biggest numbers, most flattering to Tano (she is Head of New Media at a European tech title — she is the most Tano-adjacent judge in the room). Probably the LEAST crowded. But its evidence is about access and content decisions, which is abstract and non-visual, and the gravitational pull of the case is toward a content-strategy dashboard — which fails judging criterion #1 ("value to a real audience member") harder than anything else you could build. The E-04 access ledger has no consumable objects for an audience member. High ceiling, very high risk of building something that is obviously a creator analytics tool.

CROWDING ESTIMATE with ~54 builders / maybe 12-16 teams: 001 ~40%, 002 ~35%, 003 ~25%.

NET: take 002, build Concept 1, and treat the absence of imagery as a design constraint we convert into the aesthetic. If the team is not confident it can make a monochrome dossier UI look expensive in 8 hours, take 003 and build Concept 2's mechanic there instead, where nobody expects pictures.
named_person_and_decision:
JAMIE / 29 (E-07.2: "Owns basics. Wants styling help. Returns to old posts and asks follow-ups. HIGH REPEAT"), speaking in the inbox as @laura (E-01.9: "I'm trying not to buy more stuff. Can you help me use what I own?"), @niamhh (E-01.3: "I love the outfit but I live in trainers. How would you change it?") and @maya_m (E-01.8: "I bought the shoes. What should I wear with them?").

THE DECISION, EXACTLY: It is Thursday night. Jamie has a dinner on Saturday, owns eight things he actually wears, and is stuck on "do I have to buy something, or is there already an outfit in here — and if I buy exactly one thing, which one thing unlocks the most?" Today he resolves it by scrolling back through Sofia's old posts and sending her a DM she will answer in about eleven hours, if at all. He is one of the 38 useful questions in her 14:00 DM sprint (E-02), and he is the highest-repeat, lowest-attribution person in the file: he never clicks anything, which is why the 16:00 drop says 62% of high-value purchasers never touched an affiliate link.

concepts.name: INSIDE JOB — the outfit you already own
concepts.one_liner: Jamie tells it the eight things he actually wears; Sofia's judgement runs over every possible combination of them and lights up the six she would actually wear — then shows the single £35 item that unlocks eleven more.
concepts.audience_member: JAMIE / 29 (E-07.2), voiced in the inbox by @laura (E-01.9 "I'm trying not to buy more stuff, can you help me use what I own?"), @niamhh (E-01.3 "I live in trainers, how would you change it?") and @maya_m (E-01.8 "I bought the shoes, what should I wear with them?").
concepts.decision: "Do I need to buy anything at all for Saturday — and if I buy exactly one thing, which one thing gives me the most outfits Sofia would approve of?" Today that decision is a DM Sofia answers eleven hours later.
concepts.how_it_works: Jamie taps in what he owns — eight garments, thirty seconds, no photos, no account. Plain JavaScript enumerates every structurally valid outfit from that set (one top, one bottom or dress, one shoe, optional layer), which for eight owned items is roughly 90 combinations and for the full wardrobe-plus-catalogue space is a few hundred; enumeration is free, deterministic and instant. Every single combination is then sent to Jev as its own state, carrying the garments, Sofia's verbatim notes on each from E-04, Jamie's stated life (trainers, no dry-cleaning, Saturday dinner) and Sofia's rules lifted from E-05. Each combination is judged on six parallel questions and comes back as calibrated probabilities, not sentences. The results are a matrix of atomic scores, precomputed and cached, so the interface can re-weight them in the browser with zero further inference: drag the occasion from 'everyday' to 'dinner' and the entire board re-sorts in one frame. The six highest-probability outfits are surfaced with Sofia's own words attached — the silk skirt card literally says "best with trainers" because she wrote that (E-04.3). Crucially the rejects are shown too, greyed, each stamped with the rule that killed it: the vintage leather jacket is out with "great, but warm" (E-04.2), the grey knit is flagged "soft but pills" (E-04.7). Then the drawer opens: hover any one item from Sofia's inventory and the lattice visibly grows — new nodes appear, some ignite gold — and a counter reads how many Sofia-approved outfits that one purchase buys you, and at what price each. That number, outfits-per-pound, is the recommendation. Sofia is not asleep in this product; she is the scoring function.
concepts.jev_role: Six questions per outfit, all evaluated in parallel against one shared state per combination; parallelism across combinations is achieved with concurrent HTTP requests fanned out on Modal. (1) `sofia_would_wear` — noul, criteria.true: "she would put this on without thinking, it reads like her actual uniform", criteria.false: "technically coordinated but not her eye — matchy, costumey or trying". (2) `text_my_sister` — noul, her own rule verbatim from E-05.1: "Sofia's rule is that if she would not text it to her sister she does not link it. Would she text this?" (3) `fits_this_life` — noul over the wearer's stated constraints (trainers, commute, no dry clean). (4) `occasion` — choice over {everyday, work, dinner, wedding, weekend} with the full probability distribution kept, because that distribution IS the slider. (5) `effort` — score over ["thrown on", "considered", "trying too hard"], because Sofia's taste is a penalty on the third level. (6) `rule_break` — choice over her named failure modes {too_warm (E-04.2), will_pill (E-04.7), overpriced_for_category (E-04.4), not_her_silhouette, none}, which is what produces the greyed-out reasons. Six questions × ~220 combinations = ~1,320 calibrated judgments, precomputed. The live on-stage run is only the delta when a new item is added — roughly 60 new combinations, 360 judgments, a few seconds and under a cent. Everything the sliders do afterwards is arithmetic on cached numbers: no inference, sub-frame, and it never fails on stage.
concepts.hero_visual: A dark dossier-grey board. Down the left rail, eight small type-set cards: THE THINGS YOU OWN. Filling the rest of the screen, a lattice of ~220 small squares in a loose grid, each one an outfit, each one's brightness set by Sofia's `sofia_would_wear` probability — so the board reads as a field of dim static with six squares burning gold. Above it, four sliders: OCCASION, WEATHER, EFFORT, BUDGET. A header counter: "220 OUTFITS IN YOUR WARDROBE. SOFIA WOULD WEAR 6." Click a gold square and it expands into an outfit card — three garments, a confidence bar, and one line in Sofia's own handwriting-style type: "best with trainers." Click a dim square and it expands too, struck through, with the rule that killed it: "great, but warm." Then the bottom drawer slides up — THE ONE THING — and as you hover the £35 white tee, forty-two new squares fan into the lattice in real time and eleven of them catch fire. The counter re-reads: "+11 OUTFITS. £3.18 EACH."
concepts.demo_90s:
0:00–0:30 THE TARGET. Hold up the case file. "We stole one line from Sofia's notebook that nobody else read." Read E-05.3 aloud: 'let people tell me what they already own — maybe the answer is not a shop.' "This is Jamie. He owns eight things. He does not want to buy anything. He asks Sofia what to wear with them and she answers eleven hours later, if at all. She answers that question 38 times a day." (E-02, 14:00.)
0:30–2:00 THE HEIST. Type Jamie's eight items live, out loud, fast — white tee, jeans, trainers, grey knit, black blazer. Hit enter. The lattice materialises: 220 dim squares. "Sofia's judgement just ran over every combination of your own clothes." Six ignite. Click one: the outfit, her line, 'best with trainers.' Click a dead one: 'great, but warm — you said Saturday is indoors.' "It tells you no, in her words, for her reasons. That is the part that makes it hers." Now drag OCCASION from everyday to dinner — the whole board re-sorts instantly. "No model ran just then. The judgement was already computed. Sofia is not a chatbot you wait for, she is a scoring function you can move around." Then open the drawer: "He is allowed to buy exactly one thing." Hover the £180 vintage jacket — four new outfits, one gold. Hover the £35 white tee — forty-two new squares, eleven gold. "£35 buys eleven outfits. £3.18 an outfit. The expensive thing bought him one."
2:00–3:00 THE SCORE. "At four o'clock we learned 62% of her buyers never click a link and 41% buy after sending it to a friend. This product has nothing to click. Jamie never sees a link until the moment he has already decided what he needs — one item, chosen for a reason he can repeat to a friend." Tap SEND TO A FRIEND: the outfit card becomes a dark share card with Sofia's line on it. "That is the 41%, and it is now something she can see." Close: "Sofia no longer needs to answer 'what would you wear with this' 38 times a day, because her styling judgement now runs on other people's wardrobes while she is asleep."
concepts.why_wow: Three things land in the same ten seconds. First, the board itself: the audience watches a person's own wardrobe turn into a field of hundreds of judged possibilities, which is a shape nobody has seen before and which instantly communicates 'this ran a thousand times.' Second, the sliders move the whole lattice with zero latency, which reads as impossible and is actually just arithmetic on cached Jev scores — the most Jev-native trick available and one almost nobody will exploit. Third, the £35-buys-eleven-outfits moment is a genuine gasp: it reframes a purchase as a unit of unlocked possibility, it is arithmetic anyone in the room can verify, and it is the opposite of what a shopping product is supposed to say. And the greyed-out rejections carrying Sofia's own words are what stop it reading as a matcher and make it read as taste.
concepts.commercial_potential: Three stacked revenue lines, all real. (1) THE ONE THING is the highest-conviction affiliate unit that exists: it is a single item, chosen after the person has already been shown that they do not need it, justified by a number they computed themselves. Sofia's own data says curated beats voluminous — E-03.4, the quiet winner, 28K views and 427 purchases from ONE blazer, versus E-03.2, 184K views and 92 purchases from a whole Copenhagen haul. A product that ships one recommendation instead of thirty is aimed directly at her best-converting behaviour. (2) THE WARDROBE GRAPH: every user hands over a structured inventory of what they own, voluntarily, because they get something back immediately. For a fashion creator that is the most valuable first-party dataset in the category — Sofia stops guessing what her audience needs and knows it. She can walk into the 12:30 brand call in E-02 and say '4,000 of my people own trainers and no tailoring' and negotiate a capsule against it. That dataset is what a brand actually pays for, and it is not scrapeable. (3) WHITE LABEL: Tano's business is many creators, not one. The taste layer is a swappable file of rules and notes; the lattice engine is creator-agnostic. This is a product Tano can ship to its whole roster on Monday, which is precisely the pitch that wins BEST COMMERCIAL POTENTIAL in a room owned by Tano. Pricing: free to audience, creator pays £30–100/mo or revenue-shares the single affiliate unit, brands pay for the wardrobe panel.
concepts.elegance: The division of labour is the whole design and it is clean enough to say in one sentence: CODE ENUMERATES, JEV JUDGES, THE BROWSER RE-WEIGHTS. Combinatorics is free and deterministic, so we never ask a model to do it. Judgement is the only thing a model is needed for, so that is all we ask. Re-ranking is arithmetic, so it happens in the browser at 60fps with no network. There is one screen, no login, no upload, no chat box, no generated prose anywhere in the product. The input is eight taps and the output is six outfits and one number. Nothing in it exists that could be removed.
concepts.inventiveness: Nobody else in the room will build a combinatorial lattice, because the obvious move in every case file is a recommender that ranks the creator's catalogue. This inverts the catalogue: the primary inventory is the AUDIENCE MEMBER'S, and the creator's inventory is the marginal addition. That inversion is written in Sofia's own notebook (E-05.3) and in her margin note 'people want my eye, not my inventory' (E-05.5), and I would bet nobody reads those two lines as a product spec. The derived metric — marginal Sofia-approved outfits per pound spent — does not exist in fashion commerce and is the kind of number that gets quoted back at you by a judge. And the sliders-without-inference trick turns a pile of probabilities into a live instrument, which is the Jev capability the viral demos hint at but do not actually show.
concepts.evidence_used: E-05.3 (the unfinished idea that IS this product), E-05.5 ('people want my eye, not my inventory'), E-05.4 ('stop making 100 links, curate 5' — we ship one), E-05.1 (the sister rule, used verbatim as a noul), E-04.1–E-04.8 (every item, and critically every SOFIA SAYS note, which becomes both a scoring input and the visible reason on a rejection), E-01.3 / E-01.8 / E-01.9 (the three DMs that are literally this question), E-07.2 (Jamie), E-06.1 ('capture how I think about clothes, not just what I own'), E-02 (the 14:00 sprint of 38 questions this removes), E-03.4 vs E-03.2 (one curated item outperforms a haul by 4.6x on a sixth of the reach), E-09.2 and E-09.4 (62% no click, 41% after a share).
concepts.handles_1600_drop: It was already built for it, which is the point — we do not pivot at 16:00, we point at the envelope and say 'this is why.' The drop says 62% of high-value purchasers never clicked an affiliate link; this product has essentially nothing to click, and the single link it does produce appears only after the person has decided, for a reason they can articulate. The drop says the median lag is 3.4 days; the lattice is a saved, returnable object, and a wardrobe only gets more valuable across those days, so lag is a feature rather than leakage. The drop says 2.2x conversion for people who saved 3+ looks; a saved wardrobe is a stronger and more durable signal than three saves, and it is structured rather than inferred. The drop says 41% of purchases follow a share; the share card is a styled outfit built from things the sender owns, which is a far more natural thing to send a friend than a product link, and it is the first version of that share Sofia can actually count. The one thing we ADD at 16:00 is a small instrumentation panel for the 60-second impact beat: the E-10 table rendered as behaviour, showing that U-014, U-067, U-104, U-139, U-204 and U-288 all bought with LINK CLICK = NO, and showing which of them a wardrobe would have caught.
concepts.trust_safety: The product never generates a sentence. Jev returns numbers; every word of prose on screen is either Sofia's verbatim note from E-04/E-05 or static UI copy we wrote. Nothing is ever put in her mouth, which is the cleanest possible answer to 'WOULD I TRUST IT' and to the pet peeve of generic automation that the briefs flag twice. Second: it shows its working. A panel reads SOFIA'S RULES APPLIED and lists the seven, each traced to a page of her notebook, so the judgement is auditable rather than oracular. Third, and most important, it says NO out loud — the greyed-out outfits with their reasons are the majority of the screen, and a product whose dominant output is a refusal cannot read as a sales funnel. That maps directly to E-03.5, 'Things I would never buy again', her highest-trust and lowest-revenue post. Fourth: an ASK SOFIA escape hatch on any low-confidence result routes the genuinely novel question to her real inbox, with the lattice state attached so she answers in ten seconds instead of two minutes. It makes her more present, not less — which is what she asked for in E-06.1 and what the mission statement demands ('more audience intimacy, not less').
concepts.build_risk: MEDIUM, and the risk is concentrated in one place: Jev returning undifferentiated probabilities. If every outfit scores 0.55–0.65 the lattice is grey mush and there is no demo. Test this in the FIRST HOUR with twenty hand-built combinations, before building any UI. Mitigations that work: contrastive criteria on every noul (say what a no looks like, not just a yes), put Sofia's verbatim notes into the state rather than paraphrasing them, and if spread is still poor, rank on a composite of `text_my_sister` × `effort` × `rule_break` rather than a single noul, which sharpens separation. Second risk: only 8 of 36 inventory items exist, so we synthesise ~25 more — do this as a 20-minute data-prep task with the Claude API early, in her voice, and disclose it on stage. Third risk: fan-out 429s from ~220 concurrent requests — precompute the entire demo wardrobe to a JSON file by 15:00 and run ONLY the add-one-item delta live, with the precomputed result as the silent fallback. FALLBACK LADDER: if the lattice does not separate, ship the same product with 40 hand-seeded combinations and lean the demo entirely on the add-one-item moment, which is the real WOW and needs only 60 judgments to work. If Jev is down entirely, the cached JSON demo is indistinguishable to the audience and we say so honestly.
concepts.final_line: Sofia no longer needs to answer "what would you wear with this?" 38 times a day, because her styling judgement now runs on other people's wardrobes while she is asleep.

concepts.name: THE APPRAISER — Sofia's eye, on things she has never seen
concepts.one_liner: Paste any garment on the internet, or hand it a brand's entire 200-piece lookbook, and Sofia's judgement values it in seconds — and then publishes the 196 she would refuse, with her reason on each.
concepts.audience_member: PRIYA / 31 (E-07.3: "Wants Sofia's 'buy once' judgement. Saves 'worth it' posts. HIGH AOV"), voiced in the inbox by @roisin (E-01.4: "Anything like this but under £120? I'm not paying £400 lol"), @amelie.paris (E-01.2: "if you were me, which one would you actually buy?") and @georgia (E-01.11, who was sent a coat video by her boyfriend and now has to judge a coat Sofia never linked).
concepts.decision: "There is a £400 blazer in my basket that Sofia has never mentioned. Is it worth it, or is there a version under £120 she would actually approve of?" Priya is the highest-value person in the file and she is currently stuck because Sofia's judgement only covers 36 items and the internet has four million.
concepts.how_it_works: We distil Sofia's taste into a portable dossier: her seven rules from E-05, her price ceilings inferred per category from E-04 (a tee is worth £35 and no more, shoes cross into 'expensive-ish, worth it' around £120, a jacket earns £145 only if it is tailored and neutral), and her named failure modes — too warm, will pill, trend not uniform, priced above its category, fine but the cheap version is enough. That dossier is a few hundred tokens and travels in every Jev state. Then the product takes any item Sofia has never seen — pasted from a retailer, or an entire uploaded catalogue — and runs five parallel typed questions against it. The single-item mode answers Priya in under a second with a verdict, a price verdict, and, if the verdict is negative, the specific reason and the nearest thing Sofia WOULD stand behind. The nearest thing is found not by visual similarity but by taste-vector proximity: we ask Jev which of Sofia's own items each candidate is trying to be, and the under-£120 answer to a £400 blazer is whichever cheaper item lands closest on her axes with a higher `would_link`. That is a dupe engine powered by judgement rather than by pixels, and it is a genuinely different thing. The catalogue mode is the showpiece: 200 items, 5 questions each, 1,000 calibrated judgments fanned out across Modal, finished in well under a minute for pennies. The output screen is not the four approvals. It is the 196 refusals, each with the rule that killed it, published as a browsable object — because E-03.5 says her zero-revenue 'things I would never buy again' post is her highest-trust content, and nobody has ever built a product whose main output is a creator's nos.
concepts.jev_role: Five questions per item, evaluated in parallel against one state that carries the item plus the taste dossier; scale comes from concurrent requests. (1) `would_link` — noul: "Would Sofia put her name on this?" with criteria.true "she would text this to her sister without hedging" and criteria.false "she might own it but she would not recommend it". (2) `verdict` — choice over {buy_once, worth_it_at_this_price, get_the_cheaper_version, hard_no}, each rubric written from her notebook; the probability distribution is what drives the visual, not just the argmax. (3) `price_verdict` — score over ["a steal", "fair", "expensive-ish but worth it", "good, but not THAT good"], levels lifted almost verbatim from E-04.5 and her contradiction pattern; the weighted score landing between levels is exactly the nuance a star rating destroys. (4) `why_not` — choice over her named failure modes, which produces the stamped reason on every rejection. (5) `understudy` — choice over her own 36 items: "which of Sofia's things is this trying to be?", which powers the under-£120 answer. Confidence is surfaced everywhere and low-confidence items are routed to a REFERRED TO SOFIA tray rather than guessed, which is both honest and a nice touch on stage. 200 items × 5 = 1,000 judgments, mirroring the public Jev demos almost exactly (724 ads, 40 seconds, 9 cents) — and we quote that lineage deliberately, because the hackathon is a Jev showcase and the judges will recognise the shape.
concepts.hero_visual: The refusal wall. A 200-cell grid of product cards fills the screen, all live white. A scan line sweeps left to right, and behind it 196 cells collapse to dark grey, each stamped with a short red reason — TOO WARM, WILL PILL, £35 IS ENOUGH, TREND NOT UNIFORM, NOT £400 GOOD. Four cells stay lit and float to the top. The headline counts down as it runs and settles on: "SOFIA WOULD LINK 4 OF 200. 41 SECONDS. £0.11." Beneath it a second tab, THE NOs, is the trust product: the 196 rejections, filterable by reason, which is the most Sofia-voiced screen anyone will show all day. And in the top-right corner, Priya's single-item view: the £400 blazer, its price verdict needle resting between 'expensive-ish but worth it' and 'good, but not THAT good', and directly below it the £145 black blazer with `would_link` 0.94 and Sofia's own four words — "buy once, wear forever."
concepts.demo_90s:
0:00–0:30 THE TARGET. "Sofia's judgement covers 36 items. Her audience asks about the other four million." Read E-06.1 off the sheet: 'if something could capture how I THINK about clothes — not just what I own.' "That is the whole brief and it is one sentence. Priya is about to spend £400 on a blazer Sofia has never seen."
0:30–2:00 THE HEIST. Paste the £400 blazer URL live. Under a second: the needle lands on 'good, but not THAT good', the reason reads PRICED ABOVE ITS CATEGORY, and underneath sits the £145 black blazer with her words on it. "That is not a cheaper item, it is the item her taste says is the same decision for less. £255 saved by a creator who is asleep." Then: "Now do it at scale." Drop in a 200-piece autumn lookbook from a brand that wants her. Hit run. The wall sweeps live on stage — 196 cells going dark, one after another, reasons stamping in — and it finishes in about forty seconds. "One thousand calibrated judgments. Eleven pence. Sofia would link four." Open THE NOs tab and scroll the refusals. "Her highest-trust post is the one where she tells people what NOT to buy, and it made her zero pounds. This makes that a product."
2:00–3:00 THE SCORE. "Her note says STOP MAKING 100 LINKS, CURATE 5. We just curated four out of two hundred and we did it for eleven pence, so she can do it for every brand that pitches her, every week, before she has to read a single email." Then the commercial turn: "The brand that sent this lookbook would pay to know these four before the pitch. Sofia now earns from the 196 she says no to. That has never been true for a creator before." Close on the line.
concepts.why_wow: The refusal wall is the single most watchable thing anyone will put on screen at this hackathon. It is motion, it is scale, it is legible from the back of a cafe, and it visibly represents a thousand decisions happening — which is the Jev thesis rendered as choreography rather than described. The counter landing on 'four of two hundred, forty-one seconds, eleven pence' is the exact shape of the demos that made Jev go viral, and doing it live with a creator's taste instead of ad copy is the obvious next move that nobody has made yet. And the second wow is conceptual rather than visual: a product whose primary output is a creator's NOs is genuinely surprising, it is the opposite of every affiliate tool ever built, and it is the thing a fashion creator in the audience will immediately want.
concepts.commercial_potential: The biggest ceiling of the three by a wide margin, and the one that maps onto Tano's own business. Taste becomes a licensable asset with three buyers. (1) BRANDS pay for pre-screening: a brand with 200 SKUs pays to know which four Sofia would genuinely stand behind before it wastes a pitch, and the price of that answer is eleven pence of compute against a four-figure campaign. (2) SOFIA earns from refusal, which is structurally new — at present her 'things I would never buy again' post makes £0 (E-03.5) while being her highest-trust asset; The Appraiser turns every no into a paid screening decision, which resolves her stated conflict in E-05.6 ('she keeps saying less links, but her most curated posts convert best') by making curation itself the revenue line rather than volume. (3) RETAILERS AND MARKETPLACES pay for a taste-based dupe layer: 'the under-£120 version of this' is one of the highest-intent queries in fashion commerce (@roisin, E-01.4) and everyone currently answers it with image similarity, which produces cheap lookalikes that are wrong. Answering it with a trusted human's judgement is a better product and a defensible one. And the whole thing is creator-agnostic: the taste dossier is a text file, so Tano can stand up an Appraiser for every creator on its roster and sell the network to brands as a screening layer. That is a company, not a feature.
concepts.elegance: Sofia's entire taste compresses to a few hundred tokens of dossier — seven rules, five failure modes, a price ceiling per category — and that dossier is the only thing that has to move. The product is therefore one function, item → five typed judgments, called once for a person and a thousand times for a brand, with no difference in the code path between the two. Single-item mode and catalogue mode are the same product at two scales, which is why it can serve an audience member and a business from one screen. There is no database, no embedding index, no training, no fine-tune, and no prose.
concepts.inventiveness: Two ideas nobody will bring. First, extending a creator's judgement BEYOND her own inventory — every other team in every case will build something that ranks or filters the creator's existing catalogue, because that is the data they were handed, and the one line that authorises going further (E-06.1, 'not just what I own') is easy to read as flavour text rather than as a spec. Second, and more so: making the refusals the product. Publishing the 196 nos with reasons attached is counterintuitive, commercially inverted, directly supported by her own highest-trust post making zero revenue, and it is the single strongest possible answer to 'WOULD I TRUST IT'. Also quietly novel: the understudy question turns dupe-finding into a taste-proximity problem rather than a visual-similarity problem, which is a better solution to a real and enormous commercial query.
concepts.evidence_used: E-06.1 verbatim (the mandate for judging unseen items), E-04.1–E-04.8 in full — every price, category and SOFIA SAYS note becomes a calibration anchor, with E-04.4 ('£35 is enough') and E-04.5 ('expensive-ish, worth it') defining the price-verdict scale and E-04.2/E-04.7 defining two of the five failure modes, E-05.1 (BUY / MAYBE / NO becomes the choice type, and the sister rule becomes the noul), E-05.4 ('STOP MAKING 100 LINKS. CURATE 5' — the demo curates 4 from 200), E-05.6 (the curation contradiction this resolves commercially), E-01.4 (@roisin, the under-£120 query), E-01.2 (@amelie.paris, 'which one would you actually buy'), E-01.11 (@georgia, an item Sofia never posted), E-07.3 (Priya), E-03.5 ('things I would never buy again' — high trust, zero revenue — the entire justification for THE NOs tab), and the subject-file rule 'I would rather link 3 things I truly love than 30 I was paid to post'.
concepts.handles_1600_drop: The drop says 62% never click and the median decision lag is 3.4 days, which is fatal to a link-click product and harmless to this one, because The Appraiser is consulted BEFORE the purchase and does not care where the purchase eventually happens — Priya can buy the £145 blazer in a shop three days later and the product has still done its job. The drop says 41% of purchases follow a share; a verdict card reading 'Sofia would not pay £400 for this — here is the £145 one' is dramatically more shareable than a link, because it contains an opinion and saves the recipient money, so we ship the verdict card as the atomic shareable unit. The drop says 2.2x for 3+ saves; every appraisal is saved into a personal SHORTLIST, which both matches that behaviour and gives Sofia her first view of what her audience is considering that she has never posted about — which is, incidentally, the most valuable product-research feed a fashion creator could own and another thing to sell. The honest tension we should name on stage: this concept's natural centre of gravity is commercial rather than audience-side, so at 16:00 we deliberately lead the demo with Priya's single £400 decision and let the catalogue wall be the second act, not the first.
concepts.trust_safety: Same core guarantee as Concept 1 and it matters more here: Jev does not generate, so the product never writes a sentence as Sofia. Verdicts are typed values; the words on screen are her own notes and our static labels. Beyond that: every appraisal shows which of her rules fired and links to the notebook page it came from, so a judge can audit any verdict in two clicks. Confidence is displayed rather than hidden, and anything below threshold goes to a REFERRED TO SOFIA tray instead of being answered — the product knows the edge of its own competence, which is the single most trust-building behaviour it can exhibit and takes ten lines of code. Commercial integrity is protected by construction: the brand pays for the screening, not for a yes, and the screen shows the nos as prominently as the yeses, so there is no mechanism by which money buys a verdict. We say that out loud on stage because it is the first question a creator judge will ask.
concepts.build_risk: MEDIUM-HIGH. The dominant risk is data, not code: a convincing catalogue wall needs ~200 plausible garment records with names, prices, materials and descriptions, and if they look synthetic the whole demo deflates. Budget 60–90 minutes to generate them with the Claude API in realistic retailer voice across a believable price spread, and make sure the price distribution straddles Sofia's ceilings so the verdicts actually separate. Second risk: 200 concurrent requests will hit 429s; use a Modal fan-out with a concurrency cap around 20–30, exponential backoff, and — critically — precompute the full wall to JSON by 15:00, then on stage run it live with the cached result as an invisible fallback so the sweep animation always completes. Third risk: calibration drift, where the taste dossier is too vague and 60 of 200 come back approved, which destroys the '4 of 200' headline. Test with 20 items in hour one and tighten criteria until the approval rate sits near 2–5%. FALLBACK: if the catalogue mode is shaky, single-item mode alone is a complete, fast, delightful product for Priya and takes about two hours; ship that first and treat the wall as the stretch. Do not start the wall until the single item works.
concepts.final_line: Sofia no longer needs to link a hundred things to sell five, because her eye now values everything she has never seen — and gets paid for the ninety-six she refuses.

concepts.name: THE HANDOFF — the verdict that travels
concepts.one_liner: When Ella sends a look to her sister, what arrives is not a link but Sofia's judgement, which quietly re-decides itself for whoever opens it — and for the first time the 41% of purchases that happen in someone else's group chat become visible.
concepts.audience_member: ELLA / 26 (E-07.4: "Sends outfits to friends. Friend often makes the purchase. LOW ATTRIBUTION") and, equally, the person on the other end — @sarahk's sister (E-01.5: "Sending this to my sister because she needs this exact vibe") and @georgia (E-01.11: "My bf sent me your coat video because he thinks I need it"), who is the true decider and has never in the history of creator commerce been spoken to directly.
concepts.decision: For the recipient: "Someone who knows me sent me this £400 look. It is not my size, not my budget and not my life. Do I actually want it, and what is the version of it that is mine?" For Ella: "Am I about to give my sister bad advice?" Both are currently answered by nothing at all, because the share is where every creator product stops.
concepts.how_it_works: The unit of the product is not a page, it is a verdict that recomputes. Ella hits share on a look. What travels is a dark card carrying Sofia's judgement of that look — the verdict, the confidence, the reason — plus the state it was computed from. When the recipient opens it on her phone she is not shown a shop; she is shown the verdict Ella saw, and one line: "This was decided for Ella. Want it decided for you?" Three taps — roughly my size, roughly my budget, roughly my life — and the card visibly re-computes in front of her: the same five Jev questions, the same Sofia rules, a different wearer state. Sometimes the verdict flips. When it flips to no, the card says no in Sofia's terms and offers what Sofia would say instead, which is the most trust-generating thing a shared commercial object can possibly do. Meanwhile Ella gets a receipt: her sister opened it twice, Sofia agreed with her at 0.86, and the recommendation held. Every hop is a node; a share of a share carries the chain. And behind all of it sits the instrumentation nobody currently has — a dark-social graph where a purchase at the end of a three-hop chain with zero link clicks is attributed back to the share that caused it, which is precisely the 41% and the 62% that the 16:00 envelope says are being thrown away.
concepts.jev_role: The same five atomic questions from the taste layer — `would_link`, `verdict`, `price_verdict`, `why_not`, `understudy` — re-evaluated against a state whose `wearer` block has changed, which is what makes the card morph. Then two questions unique to this concept and unique in the room. (1) `right_for_recipient` — noul over a state containing BOTH people: "Sofia knows the sender knows the recipient. Given what the sender chose to send and what the recipient has told us, would Sofia endorse this for the recipient specifically?" with criteria.true "she would say yes, your friend is right about you" and criteria.false "she would gently tell them their friend is projecting". (2) `send_reason` — choice over {they_need_this_exact_thing, they_need_this_vibe, this_is_a_joke, they_asked_me_to_look}, which is read from the sender's own note and changes the card's whole tone. For the graph act we replay the twelve users of E-10 through the same questions and score each chain for share-attributable value. Total judgments in the demo are modest, a few hundred, but the shape is new: Jev is being used on a RELATIONSHIP, judging a pair rather than an object, which is not something anyone has shown.
concepts.hero_visual: Split screen, two phones. On the left, Ella's thread — she taps send and a dark card slides into an iMessage-shaped bubble. On the right, her sister's phone receives it. The card reads: VERDICT — BUY ONCE, 0.91, "buy once, wear forever." Then the sister taps three chips — UK 12 / under £150 / mostly trainers — and the card does something no shared link has ever done: it visibly re-computes on screen, the confidence bar draining from 0.91 down to 0.34, the verdict flipping to GET THE CHEAPER VERSION, and a second card sliding up beneath it with the £145 blazer and Sofia's words. Then cut to the wall behind it: the E-10 cohort rendered as a network — twelve nodes, share edges, and six purchase markers glowing at the ends of chains where the LINK CLICK column reads NO. A single counter underneath: "£4,180 OF PURCHASES YOUR DASHBOARD DOES NOT SEE."
concepts.demo_90s:
0:00–0:30 THE TARGET. Hold up the 16:00 envelope. "Forty-one percent of Sofia's purchases happen after someone sends her content to a friend. Sixty-two percent of her buyers never touch a link. So the most valuable person in her business is someone she has never met, who was sent something by someone she has never met either." Point at E-07.4. "Ella sends. Her friend buys. Sofia sees nothing."
0:30–2:00 THE HEIST. "Sofia's own rule is that if she would not text it to her sister she does not link it." (E-05.1.) "So we built the text to the sister." Ella taps share, live. The card lands on the second phone. "That is not a link. It is a judgement, and it knows it was made for the wrong person." Tap the three chips. The card re-computes on screen, confidence visibly draining from 0.91 to 0.34. "Sofia just told her sister no. On a shared shopping link. And then told her what to buy instead." Beat. "That is the entire trust problem in creator commerce solved in one animation — the thing that travels is not a sales pitch, it is an opinion that will change its mind about you." Then flip to Ella's receipt: "Sofia agreed with you."
2:00–3:00 THE SCORE. Bring up the graph. "These are the twelve people in the four o'clock file. Every glowing chain ends in a purchase and starts with a share. Not one of them clicked a link. Today all of that is attributed to nobody." Counter lands. "Sofia can now see the half of her business that is invisible — and, more importantly, the friend at the end of the chain finally got a real answer instead of a forwarded advert." Close on the line.
concepts.why_wow: One animation carries the entire idea: a shared shopping card changing its own mind about you, in public, in real time, and talking you out of a purchase. It is four seconds long, it needs no explanation, and it is emotionally surprising in a way that a grid or a chart is not. The second wow is the graph reveal, which visualises money that everyone in the room has just been told exists and nobody can see — that is a genuinely dramatic beat to land at the end of a demo, and it is the direct payoff of the envelope the whole room watched being opened.
concepts.commercial_potential: The highest ceiling of the three and the most speculative. Dark-social attribution is a category, not a feature — it is the thing every affiliate network, every creator platform and every DTC brand has been unable to measure for a decade, and the standard estimate of the gap is exactly the order of magnitude the envelope states. A product that instruments the share by making the share USEFUL to the recipient — rather than by tracking them — sidesteps the privacy problem that has killed every prior attempt, because the recipient volunteers their context in exchange for a better answer. If it works, the business is not a creator tool, it is an attribution layer sold per-share to networks and brands, with the creator taking a cut of purchases that previously attributed to nobody. Near-term and concretely for Tano: it converts a creator's most valuable and least monetisable audience segment into a tracked, addressable one, which is precisely the pitch Tano makes to brands. The risk is that it is a two-sided network product, and two-sided network products are the hardest thing to prove in a demo and the hardest to bootstrap in reality.
concepts.elegance: The insight is a single substitution — replace the link with the judgement — and everything else follows from it mechanically. The same five atomic questions from the taste layer are reused unchanged; only the wearer block in the state differs, which is why the card can morph with no new code. Attribution is not a tracking system bolted on, it is a side effect of the card being worth opening: the recipient identifies themselves because doing so gets them a better answer. Nothing is surveilled, nothing is fingerprinted, and there is no cookie in it.
concepts.inventiveness: This is the one nobody in the room will build, and I am fairly confident of that. Every team on all three cases will build a product for the creator or for the follower. This builds for the person the follower sends it to — a person who appears in three separate exhibits (E-01.5, E-01.11, E-07.4), is named as the actual purchaser, and is structurally invisible to every existing tool. Using Jev to judge a PAIR of people rather than an object is also novel: `right_for_recipient` is a question about a relationship, evaluated with calibration, which is a genuinely new use of the primitive and exactly the sort of thing the Jev team would be delighted to see. And the product's most memorable moment is it talking someone OUT of a purchase, which no commerce product does.
concepts.evidence_used: E-09.4 (41% of purchases follow a share — the whole thesis), E-09.2 (62% never clicked), E-10 in full — the twelve-row table is rendered directly as the attribution graph, with the SHARES and LINK CLICK columns doing the dramatic work, E-05.1 (the sister rule, which the product literally instantiates), E-01.5 (@sarahk sending to her sister), E-01.11 (@georgia, sent a coat by her boyfriend), E-07.4 (Ella, LOW ATTRIBUTION), E-04 (every item's price, size and SOFIA SAYS note, used to re-decide for the recipient), E-01.4 and E-01.6 (the budget and size chips the recipient taps), and the briefing note that "the strongest product may serve a decision, a taste system, or a SOCIAL BEHAVIOUR rather than a shopping link".
concepts.handles_1600_drop: It is the drop, turned into a product — which is both its greatest strength and its greatest strategic risk. The entire concept is the direct implementation of E-09.4 and E-10, so at 16:00 we have nothing to change and everything to point at, and the 60-second impact beat writes itself from the envelope. The strategic risk is the mirror image: if we build this before 16:00 we are betting on the contents of a sealed envelope, and if we build it after 16:00 we have two hours. The honest play is to build the taste layer (shared with Concept 2) in the morning, which is useful under any envelope, and decide at 16:01 whether to spend the last two hours on the share card. The card itself is maybe ninety minutes of work on top of an existing taste layer. The graph is another hour and is the part to cut.
concepts.trust_safety: This is the concept where trust is the product rather than a constraint, and the demo's central moment is the system refusing a sale. A shared card that tells the recipient "this is not right for you, here is what is" cannot be mistaken for automation or for an advert; it behaves like a friend with taste, which is precisely how the case file describes Sofia's relationship with her audience. On privacy, which a judge will absolutely raise: nothing is tracked. The recipient is never fingerprinted, never cookied and never identified — they tap three chips voluntarily because tapping them gets them a better answer, and the attribution is a consequence of participation rather than of surveillance. The sender sees only whether their recommendation held, never the recipient's details. And as with the others, Jev generates nothing: the words are Sofia's own notes and our static UI. Say all of this in one sentence on stage, because it is the difference between this reading as a clever attribution hack and reading as a product a creator would actually put in her bio.
concepts.build_risk: HIGH — the highest of the three, and the reason it is ranked third despite being the most inventive. Two surfaces (sender and recipient), a live state handoff between them, a morphing card animation, and a network graph is a lot for eight hours, and the demo requires two devices or two browser windows staying in sync on a cafe wifi network, which is a classic live-demo failure. Hard mitigations: no real backend — encode the state in the URL fragment so the handoff is a link with no server, which removes sync failure entirely; precompute both the before and after verdicts so the morph is a cached animation rather than a live call, with one genuine live call kept for authenticity; and build the whole thing as one page with two phone frames side by side rather than two actual devices, which is also a better stage visual. FALLBACK LADDER: if time runs out, cut the graph and ship the morphing card alone — that is the emotional core and it is about ninety minutes on top of the shared taste layer. If the card is at risk, the taste layer from Concept 2 is a complete product on its own. Do not start this one before 16:00 unless the taste layer is already finished.
concepts.final_line: Sofia no longer needs to be in the group chat, because her verdict travels with the share and re-decides itself for whoever opens it.

case_strength_assessment:
PICK IT — but only with a differentiator, because it is the crowded case.

Why 001 is the strongest evidence-to-product conversion of the three:
(1) It is the ONLY case with a numeric subjective rating column. E-04 gives every product a Maya score (9.6 SPF, 9.5 Red Reset, 8.1 Glass Drop) AND a one-line note. Case 002's wardrobe has notes but no numbers; case 003 has no inventory at all. Numbers + notes = a typed judgement space Jev can be run over thousands of times and code can re-weight instantly. That is precisely the shape our stack is best at.
(2) It is the ONLY case with E-02.2, an explicit written routing tree (DRY -> Cloud Cream + Barrier Oil, OILY -> Daily Gel, SENSITIVE -> avoid fragrance, REDNESS -> Red Reset, shade questions = ask current foundation) plus her literal intake questions in E-02.1 and a hard guardrail in E-02.4 ("DO NOT RECOMMEND RETINOL TO EVERYONE"). Cases 002/003 only have "questions I keep answering". We can ship a product whose every branch is traceable to a line of evidence — free marks on "use of the evidence" and "fidelity to her voice".
(3) It is the ONLY case with E-08 DISCOUNTED LEADS, which explicitly lists the five wrong answers (DM bot, the 74K post, the £62 serum, the noisy customer, and the undervalued silent customer). That is a free scoring rubric. Half the room will build E-08.1, the thing the dossier already told them is wrong.
(4) Skincare is a small closed domain (10 SKUs, 5 skin types, 6 finishes, a budget axis). An 8-hour build can genuinely be COMPLETE rather than a stub. Nothing has to be faked or sourced.
(5) It has the clearest single named audience member with a decision she is measurably stuck on (Priya, sensitive skin), which the brief makes a hard gate.

The honest weaknesses:
- MOST CROWDED. 001 is listed first, has the most legible brief, and "beauty quiz -> product recommendation" is the single most obvious hackathon build in existence. Of ~54 builders expect the largest cluster here, and expect 6-10 near-identical skin-quiz apps. If we build the obvious thing we lose on differentiation even if we execute best.
- The shelf is tiny. 10 products means the recommendation space itself is small and unimpressive; a 10-item recommender does not produce a WOW. Our scale has to come from the AUDIENCE axis, not the product axis — thousands of states, not thousands of SKUs. Every concept below is built on that correction.
- Maya is 50K/beauty; the judge with the most institutional buying power is arguably Aditi (Head of New Media, case 003). Commercial-potential judging may skew toward whoever pitches something a media company could deploy on Monday.
- Case 002 (Sofia) is a near structural clone of 001 with weaker data (no numeric ratings, no discounted-leads sheet) and a hidden cost: fashion demands imagery we do not have and would burn an hour sourcing. Do not pick 002 — it is 001 with less evidence and more asset work.
- Case 003 (Aditi) is the contrarian pick: least crowded, best retrodiction dataset (3.9M views -> 62 sign-ups vs 320K -> 806), most senior judge, and the drop is most dramatic there (71%, 9.2-day lag). But it has no typed inventory, "what should I make next" resolves to a dashboard, and machine-generated career advice is the hardest thing to make feel trustworthy in 90 seconds. Higher variance, higher ceiling.

Net: take 001. Its evidence density is the highest and its build risk is the lowest, which matters more than crowding WHEN we have a differentiator the crowd cannot copy. Ours is: Jev physically cannot generate text, so our product cannot put words in Maya's mouth — it can only choose between sentences she already wrote — and calibrated judgement is cheap enough that we show her judgement as a VISIBLE OBJECT rather than as a chat reply. If we are not willing to build that, pick 003 instead.
named_person_and_decision:
PRIYA, 31 — "SENSITIVE SKIN" (Known Associates, Sheet 04/17): "Every time I try something new my face freaks out." Needs reassurance + compatibility.

The exact decision she is stuck on: Maya's Night Serum content is everywhere and Priya's friends are buying it. Priya has roughly £35 and one free slot in her routine, and she has to decide whether to introduce the Night Serum (£42, "Best for texture") or whether that is the exact thing that will set her face off again — and if not that, then which one product she should introduce instead. Today the only route to that answer is a DM and a wait: by E-05 she is one of 6,219 people asking "what should I buy?" against 1,847 Maya answered personally. So the real decision is a NO decision: what should I not buy, and what is the safe single move.

The evidence already contains Maya's answer. E-02.2 routes SENSITIVE -> avoid fragrance and REDNESS -> Red Reset. E-04.3 is Red Reset, £32, Serum, Sensitive, Calm, Maya 9.5, "For angry skin days." E-02.4 carries the hard guardrail "DO NOT RECOMMEND RETINOL TO EVERYONE". E-04.5 SPF 50 at 9.6 is "Non-negotiable". Maya has already decided; Priya just has no way to reach the decision without reaching Maya.

Secondary named person, kept in frame because of the 16:00 drop: ALEX, 28 — "SILENT BROWSER. Saves almost everything. Sends almost nothing. High intent, low visible engagement." E-08.5 flags her as potentially more valuable than the loud customer and E-09.2 confirms it — 61% of repeat buyers sent no DM before purchase. Alex will never ask. Any product that requires a question does not serve her.

concepts.name: DEAD DROP — Maya already answered. Go and collect it.
concepts.one_liner: Maya's judgement, pre-computed into ~400 calibrated verdicts and left where her audience can pick it up — so Priya gets Maya's actual recommendation, including Maya's actual refusals, in nine seconds, without ever sending a DM.
concepts.audience_member: Priya, 31, sensitive skin (Known Associates, Sheet 04/17). Also serves Emily (budget ceiling), Hannah (too many options), Grace (five minutes, two things) and, critically, Alex the silent browser who will never ask a question at all.
concepts.decision: "Do I introduce the Night Serum everyone is talking about, or will it wreck my face — and if not that, what is the one thing I should buy at £35?" Today that decision requires a DM and a wait. Dead Drop turns it into a nine-second, evidence-traceable verdict that includes the NO.
concepts.how_it_works: A dead drop is where a spy leaves the answer in advance so the two people never have to meet — exactly what E-09 asks for: help someone decide confidently before they ever need to ask Maya. Before the demo we enumerate an audience lattice from Maya's own intake questions in E-02.1: skin type (dry / oily / combo / sensitive / redness-prone) x budget band (£20 / £35 / £50 / £70 / £100) x what you already own (nothing / cleanser only / has the Night Serum / full routine) x finish preference (rich / light / calm / glow / invisible) x her last question, "do you actually care about skincare or do you just want to look hot tomorrow?" (project / tomorrow). We sample ~400 representative cells rather than the full cross product. For each cell we send ONE Jev request whose state is that audience profile plus the entire E-04 shelf including her ratings and verbatim notes, and whose questions map the whole row at once. The result is a stored lattice of roughly 4,800 calibrated atomic judgements — a JSON file, no server, no inference at demo time. The front end is then pure code: Priya taps through Maya's five questions in Maya's own words, we look up the cell, the verdict is instant. Every constraint control — budget, "only 2 products, I will not do 8 steps" (E-01.9 @joanna), "I already have the night serum" (E-01.5 @jessica) — re-weights and re-selects from the cached lattice in milliseconds with zero further inference. The verdict screen has three parts: THE PICK (one product, Maya's verbatim note, a conviction bar from Jev's probability), THE SECOND THING (shown only if the budget genuinely supports it — Grace gets exactly two), and THE REFUSALS, what Maya would tell you to skip with her own words attached: Glass Drop, greyed out, "Good. Not £62 good." E-02.4's retinol rule is a hard-coded guardrail that overrides the model and is displayed as a visible lock. Then one button: SEND THIS TO A FRIEND, which emits a card — because E-09.4 says 41% of high-value buyers arrived through a private share.
concepts.jev_role: One request per lattice cell, 12 questions per request, evaluated in parallel against one shared state. State = {profile: the audience cell drawn from E-02.1's questions, shelf: all ten E-04 rows with price / type / skin / finish / Maya rating / Maya note, rules: E-02.2's routing tree and E-02.4's retinol guardrail}. Questions: (1) `pick` — a CHOICE over all ten products, instructions "Which single product would Maya tell THIS person to buy first?", criteria = the ten products each described by its own E-04 row. This one question returns the full probability distribution across the shelf, i.e. an entire heatmap row, plus a confidence number. (2) `veto_<ref>` — ten NOULs, one per product, instructions "Would Maya actively tell this person NOT to buy this?", criteria true: "She would warn them off it — wrong skin type, wrong price for the value, or she does not rate it enough to spend this person's money on it", false: "She would be comfortable with them buying it." Calibrated by putting her Glass Drop contradiction (8.1, £62, "Good. Not £62 good.") in the state so the model learns her actual standard. (3) `enough` — a SCORE, instructions "After this answer, how confident is this person?", criteria ["Still needs to DM Maya", "Would search a bit more", "Would save it and come back", "Would buy now"], which drives the confidence bar and the demo's closing metric. Total: 12 judgements per cell x ~400 cells = ~4,800 judgements, one Modal fan-out, pennies, run once before the demo. At demo time: zero Jev calls. That is the point — it is instant because Maya already answered.
concepts.hero_visual: THE LATTICE. Full bleed, near-black, a wall of 400 rows x 10 columns. Each cell is a small square coloured by Jev's probability — cold slate near zero, a warm amber-to-white ramp toward one — with a thin diagonal hatch overlaid on vetoed cells. It materialises column by column, like a code wall resolving. Small monospace in the corner: "4,812 judgements · £0.31 · Maya typed none of them." Then you click one row and the wall pulls apart and zooms into a single card: PRIYA / SENSITIVE / £35 — a hero tile for Red Reset, £32, conviction 0.91, her line "For angry skin days" set in a handwriting weight, and directly beneath, in muted red, NIGHT SERUM — SKIP, with the routing rule cited. Two screens, one object: the whole stolen brain, then one person's answer inside it.
concepts.demo_90s:
30s THE TARGET — Put the notebook page on screen: E-02.2, her routing tree, and E-02.3 in her own hand: "Need to turn all this into something people can use without me answering 200 questions a day." Say: "We did not steal Maya's product list. Anyone can copy a product list. We stole her refusals. This is Priya. Sensitive skin. Every time she tries something new her face freaks out. She wants the Night Serum because everyone is talking about it. Maya already knows the answer for her. Priya has no way to get it without joining a queue of 6,219 people."

90s THE HEIST — Open Dead Drop in a phone frame. Five taps, Maya's own five questions, ten seconds: sensitive / redness / using a cleanser / £35 / calm. The verdict lands on the same frame as the tap, no spinner: RED RESET, £32, conviction 0.91, "For angry skin days." Then the move that wins the room: scroll to WHAT MAYA WOULD TELL YOU TO SKIP. Night Serum, greyed, with the rule cited. Glass Drop, greyed, with her verbatim "Good. Not £62 good." Say: "That is the product. It is not what she would sell you, it is what she would stop you buying." Drag the budget from £35 to £70 — the shelf reorders live, a second recommendation appears, still no loading, because nothing is being generated. Tap SEND TO A FRIEND; a card slides out. Then pinch out to THE LATTICE and let the wall fill the screen. "Every one of those is a decision Maya does not have to make again. It cost thirty-one pence."

60s THE SCORE — Numbers straight from the file: "6,219 people asked what should I buy. Maya answered 1,847. Almost everything Priya needed was already written down in Maya's notebook and on her shelf — it just had to be somewhere Priya could reach. Dead Drop answers all 6,219 before they ask, in Maya's own sentences. And it cannot do anything else: the model we used physically cannot generate text. Every word Priya reads, Maya wrote. That is why it still feels like her." Then the judging question asked the way the brief demands: "Maya — of the ten things on your shelf, is there one you would be uncomfortable seeing recommended here?" and change it live.
concepts.why_wow: Three shocks in ninety seconds. First it is INSTANT — in a room where every other demo has a spinner and a streaming chat reply, a verdict that lands on the same frame as the tap reads as a different category of product. Second it says NO out loud, with the creator's own words attached, which is the opposite of what an AI product is expected to do and the strongest trust signal available in this case file. Third, the lattice reveal reframes the thing from "a quiz" to "we extracted a person's judgement and you are looking at all of it at once" — 4,800 calibrated decisions for thirty-one pence, on screen, as an object.
concepts.commercial_potential: This is Tano's actual business shape, which matters because Tano staff are judging. The unit is a creator's judgement productised as an owned, portable asset — not a link-in-bio, not a chatbot. Who pays: (a) creators on SaaS, £99/mo at 50K rising to £499/mo above 250K, because it converts unpaid DM labour (70+ hrs/month for Maya) into an asset that earns while she sleeps; (b) affiliate revenue share on the conversions it creates, which is the real money — E-03.5 shows one post producing 317 affiliate conversions and E-09.3 says top-decile savers convert 2.4x, so the product's whole job is moving savers over the line; (c) brands, indirectly and deliberately: shelf placement is earned, never bought, which is exactly why the shelf retains value. The moat is the lattice — expensive in judgement, not compute, and it must be rebuilt whenever her taste moves, which makes it a subscription rather than a one-off. Scaling is clean: the identical pipeline runs on Sofia's wardrobe or Aditi's access ledger with no new logic, because it only ever needs an inventory with a subjective layer. Beachhead: the ~100k mid-tier commerce creators who have taste and no team.
concepts.elegance: The entire product is one idea: a creator's judgement is a LOOKUP, not a conversation. Everything follows. Because it is a lookup it is instant. Because it is precomputed it costs pennies and cannot fail live. Because Jev returns judgements rather than text, the product is physically incapable of inventing a Maya sentence — it can only choose among sentences she already wrote, so voice fidelity is structural rather than prompted. Because probabilities are numbers, the budget slider is arithmetic over a cached array rather than a new inference. No LLM, no RAG, no agent, no chat window. The brief says you do not get extra points for complexity; this is the version with the fewest moving parts that could possibly work, and every part is visible on stage.
concepts.inventiveness: Nobody else will invert the recommender. The room will build "quiz in, product out", which is E-08.1 with extra steps. The inversions here: the refusal list is the feature rather than an edge case; the answer exists before the question, so the silent browser who never asks is served identically to the person who does; and the recommendation space is rendered as a single physical object — the lattice — instead of dribbled out one chat reply at a time. The deepest move is treating "no generation" as a product guarantee and saying it out loud to a creator whose stated pet peeve is generic automation.
concepts.evidence_used: E-02.1 supplies the literal five intake questions, used verbatim as the UI. E-02.2 supplies the routing tree, shipped as declared rules inside the Jev state. E-02.4 supplies the retinol guardrail, shipped as a hard override. E-04 (all ten rows) is the shelf; price / skin / finish drive the lattice axes and Maya's rating and note pass through to the screen untouched. E-04.6 is the demo's money shot. E-01.5, E-01.9 and E-01.12 become the three constraint controls (already own it / only two products / "the one you would buy if you were me"). E-05.3 and E-05.4 (6,219 asked, 1,847 answered) are the closing arithmetic. E-06.1 is the design brief: "still getting my recommendation, even when I am not personally typing the answer." E-07.4 is the thesis on a sticky note: "People do not need more products. They need confidence." E-08.1 and E-08.3 are what we deliberately did not build.
concepts.handles_1600_drop: It survives without a rewrite because it was already built for the invisible audience, but the drop hands us two live additions inside the 30-minute window. First, framing: E-09.5's 4.6-day median lag and E-09.2's 61%-no-DM finding turn the headline from "faster answers" into "the answer is already there, days before you decide" — which is literally what a dead drop is. Second, build: E-09.4's 41%-via-private-share becomes the SEND TO A FRIEND card, and E-10 becomes a second surface. We take its ten rows — Rina, Alice, Tara, Zoe and Mila all bought with ZERO DMs — and run each through the lattice to show the product serves exactly the people who would never have spoken to Maya. The line we add: "Six of the ten highest-value people in this file never sent a DM. A better inbox would have reached none of them. This reaches all of them."
concepts.trust_safety: Four structural defences, all demonstrable rather than claimed. (1) The model cannot generate text. Jev returns probabilities and selections; every word on screen is a verbatim Maya quote from E-02 or E-04, and we say that on stage. There is no mechanism by which it can put a sentence in her mouth. (2) It refuses. A product that tells you not to buy the £62 serum is not a sales funnel, and the refusal carries her own words so the no sounds like her. (3) It never simulates a conversation. No chat bubble, no "Hi, I'm Maya's AI", no typing indicator — a verdict card, the way a review is a verdict card. Nobody feels handed to a machine because nobody is talking to anything. (4) It is editable and auditable: the lattice is a table Maya can open, filter and override, and the demo ends by inviting her to veto a cell live. E-02.4 ships as a hard rule precisely to show her stated boundaries beat the model.
concepts.build_risk: Low, and front-loaded. The real work is the lattice generation script (one Modal fan-out, ~400 requests of 12 questions each) plus a static front end reading one JSON file. Nothing runs at demo time, so the demo cannot fail from rate limits, network or latency. Three risks and mitigations: (a) 429s during generation — run it once around 14:00 with exponential backoff; it is re-runnable in minutes. (b) Jev's picks disagreeing with Maya's routing tree — validate against E-02.2 as a golden set (sensitive must never get Night Serum, dry must get Cloud Cream, everyone gets SPF 50) and tighten criteria until it passes; that is a 30-minute loop, not a research project. (c) rendering 4,000 cells smoothly — use canvas, or pre-render to an image and animate a mask. Fallback if generation fails: drop to 40 cells covering the six named personas, which demos identically, and generate the rest live since a single call is 873ms. Fallback if Jev is down entirely: the JSON is already on disk; the demo is a static file.
concepts.final_line: Maya no longer needs to answer "what should I buy" because she already answered it — 4,812 times, in her own sentences, including every time the answer was don't.

concepts.name: STAKEOUT — surveillance on the audience that never speaks
concepts.one_liner: Before Maya posts, 200 reconstructed members of her audience read the draft and Jev judges in parallel who saves it, who privately sends it to a friend, who buys without asking — and who is left with no choice but to DM her; then she edits one sentence and watches the DM debt collapse.
concepts.audience_member: Alex, 28 — the silent browser (Known Associates, Sheet 04/17): "Saves almost everything. Sends almost nothing. High intent, low visible engagement." E-08.5 flags her as potentially more valuable than the loud customer and E-09.2 proves it: 61% of repeat buyers sent no DM before purchase. Alex will never ask a question, so the only way to serve her is to answer her inside the post itself. Priya is served the same way — the caption now names her skin type before she has to.
concepts.decision: Two decisions on one screen. Maya's: "which version of this caption do I publish?" Alex's: "do I have enough to act on, or do I have to go and ask?" Stakeout makes the second decision visible so Maya can fix it before she posts, which is the only way to help a person who will never speak.
concepts.how_it_works: We reconstruct a synthetic audience — 200 ghosts — grounded in the file rather than invented. The six named personas on Sheet 04 give the archetypes; the ten rows of E-10 give real behavioural fingerprints (DMs sent, saves, shares, returns, lag, order value); the four tracked journeys in E-05.5 give the temporal shapes (Rina returned after 4 days; Alice never DM'd, saved 7 posts over 3 weeks, bought Cloud Cream + SPF; Naomi got her answer and still did not buy). Each ghost is a small typed record: skin type, budget, routine depth, DM propensity, save propensity, share propensity, patience. Maya pastes a draft caption or picks one of the six real posts from E-03. We fan out across Modal: one Jev request per ghost, four questions in parallel against a state holding {that ghost, the draft, the E-04 shelf}. 200 ghosts x 4 questions = 800 calibrated judgements in about forty seconds for a few pence. Results render as an invisible funnel — not views and likes, which E-03 already proved are lies, but SAVE / PRIVATE SHARE / ACT WITHIN 7 DAYS / STILL HAS TO ASK YOU. The headline number is DM DEBT: how many of the 200 this post leaves with an unanswered question, extrapolated against her 50K. Then the interaction that lands the demo: Maya edits one line — adds the price, names the skin type, or adds the thing she would not buy — and re-runs. DM debt falls, private shares rise, and you can see exactly which ghosts flipped. Before any of that we establish credibility by retrodiction: run the six real E-03 posts and show the predicted ranking reproduces what actually happened, including that the 74K-view post is not the winner and the 18K-view "5-minute morning routine" with 4.6K saves and 317 affiliate conversions is.
concepts.jev_role: One request per ghost, four questions, all parallel against one shared state. State = {ghost: {age, skin, budget, routine, the persona line quoted verbatim from Sheet 04, behavioural fingerprint from the matching E-10 row}, post: the draft caption, shelf: the E-04 rows it references}. Questions: (1) `save` — NOUL, "Would this person save this post to come back to later?", criteria true: "Useful to them specifically; not ready to act today but they want it findable", false: "They scroll past; it is not about their situation." (2) `share_privately` — NOUL, "Would this person send this to one specific friend in a private message?", criteria true: "They can name the exact friend this is for", false: "Not personal enough to forward." This is the money question because E-09.4 says 41% of high-value buyers arrived that way and no analytics tool on earth measures it. (3) `act_unaided` — NOUL, "Could this person decide and buy within a week WITHOUT asking Maya a question first?", criteria true: "The post already answers their specific blocker", false: "There is a gap only Maya could fill." (4) `residual_question` — CHOICE over the twelve intent categories the file already labelled in E-01 (INFO, RECOMMENDATION, JUDGEMENT, VALUE, CONTEXT, DIAGNOSIS, TRUST, RELATIONSHIP, CONSTRAINT, DELAYED INTENT, TRANSFER OF TRUST, PERSONALISATION), instructions "If this person still has to message Maya after reading this, which kind of question is it?" — so Maya sees not just how many DMs the post creates but WHICH, e.g. "this caption generates 140 VALUE questions", fixable by putting the price in. 800 judgements per run, two or three runs live, ~40 seconds each, single-digit pence total. An optional fifth SCORE for confidence level is the first thing cut if latency bites.
concepts.hero_visual: Two panels. Left: a 20x10 grid of 200 small circles on near-black, one per ghost, tinted by persona. As results stream in they resolve — filled amber for save, a thin outbound arrow drawn between circles for a private share, solid white for acts-without-asking, a hollow red ring for still-has-to-ask. Watching 200 dots resolve in a wave over forty seconds is the visual that made the public Jev demos travel. Right: the invisible funnel as four descending horizontal bars and, above it in very large monospace, the DM DEBT counter. The demo peak: Maya adds one sentence, we re-run, and the counter animates 214 -> 41 while eleven red rings flip to white and private-share arrows multiply across the grid. Behind it, faint: "None of these people were ever going to message you."
concepts.demo_90s:
30s THE TARGET — Put E-03 on screen. "Her biggest post: 74,000 views. Her best post: 18,000 views, 4,600 saves, 317 sales. Her own file says read the behaviour, not the vanity metric. The problem is that the behaviour that matters — saving, privately sending it to a friend, coming back four days later — is invisible to every tool she owns. This is Alex. She saves everything and sends nothing, and 61% of Maya's repeat buyers look like her. Alex is never going to ask a question, so the answer has to already be in the post."

90s THE HEIST — Credibility beat first: run the six real E-03 posts. The predicted order matches the real order; the 74K post comes fourth. "We did not tune this. It read the posts the way her audience did." Now paste tomorrow's draft caption. Hit RUN STAKEOUT. Two hundred dots resolve live in a wave — let it breathe, this is the shot. Funnel fills. DM DEBT: 214. Click the red rings; they cluster into VALUE and DIAGNOSIS. "A hundred and forty of these people are about to ask you the same thing: is it actually worth it." Now edit one sentence in the caption — add "£32, and skip it if you're oily" — and re-run. DM DEBT 214 -> 41. Private shares up 2.3x. "One sentence. She just answered a hundred and seventy DMs before anyone sent them."

60s THE SCORE — "Maya spends 70 hours a month replying. We did not make the replies faster, because her own file says that is the wrong answer. We made the post do the replying. And the thing being measured is the thing nobody can measure: whether Alex sends this to her sister. Four judgements per person, two hundred people, eleven pence, forty seconds." Then the brief's question, asked properly: "Maya — look at the forty-one it says still have to ask you. Is it right about them?"
concepts.why_wow: Watching 200 dots resolve in parallel is the exact aesthetic of the Jev demos that travelled, and it is impossible to fake with an LLM in a hackathon. But the real shock is the retrodiction beat: a tool that correctly predicts, from captions alone, that the 74K-view post underperformed the 18K-view one — in front of the creator who lived it — buys total credibility in twelve seconds, and "does it work" is a stated judging criterion almost nobody else will be able to evidence. Then DM DEBT hands the room a number it has never seen: the cost, in unanswered questions, of a sentence you forgot to write. The one-sentence edit collapsing 214 to 41 is the most literal possible execution of "show how it makes their life easier".
concepts.commercial_potential: The largest business of the three and the most obviously Tano-shaped: pre-publish intelligence for creator-led commerce — know before you post.
