Who pays: (a) creators on SaaS, £49/mo solo up to £399/mo for teams, pitched as one saved hour a week against Maya's 70 hours a month; (b) creator agencies and talent management, seat-based, because they currently run zero pre-publish QA and manage dozens of Mayas; (c) brands and their agencies at the real money end — a brand briefing 40 creators can test 40 caption variants against each creator's OWN reconstructed audience before a penny of paid spend, a category currently served by nothing, priced per campaign rather than per seat; (d) the derived asset is the durable one: over months Stakeout accumulates a calibrated model of each creator's invisible funnel — the save-to-share-to-buy graph no platform exposes — which is a genuine data moat and, notably, exactly the intelligence Tano needs to price creator deals. Unit economics are absurd in our favour: ~£0.05 of inference per prediction against a placement decision worth thousands. It generalises unchanged: swap the ghosts and it runs on Sofia's audience or Aditi's 42K newsletter.
concepts.elegance: It replaces a dashboard with a jury. Analytics answers "what happened"; this answers "what would happen", and it does so by asking two hundred specific people four plain questions rather than by fitting a model to a metric. The whole system is one loop — ghost + draft in, four probabilities out, aggregate, render — run two hundred times, and its correctness is checkable against evidence the organisers handed us. No training, no embeddings, no vector store, no prompt chain. The elegance claim for the stage: the only reason this was impossible last year is that asking two hundred people four questions used to cost two hundred people.
concepts.inventiveness: Nobody in the room will build a tool that predicts the metrics you cannot see; every other team will optimise a number the platform already reports. Stakeout's four outputs — saves, PRIVATE shares, acts-without-asking, residual question type — are precisely the four things E-09 says drive the business and precisely the four things no dashboard contains. Two further inventions: DM DEBT as a unit, treating an unanswered question as a liability the post incurred, which reframes content quality as debt avoidance; and using the twelve intent labels the case file itself printed in E-01 as the CHOICE criteria, so residual questions come back typed in Maya's own taxonomy. The retrodiction check — validating a predictive product against evidence the organisers supplied — reads as rigour in a room running on vibes.
concepts.evidence_used: Sheet 04's six personas are the ghost archetypes, quoted verbatim into the Jev state so judgement is grounded in the file's own language. E-10's ten behavioural rows (DM / saves / shares / return / buy / lag / order value) are the fingerprints we sample; E-05.5's four tracked journeys (Rina, Megan, Alice, Naomi) set the temporal patterns. E-03's six posts, with views / likes / saves / comments and the 317 affiliate conversions on E-03.5, are the retrodiction test set. E-01's twelve labelled intent categories are the literal criteria of the residual-question CHOICE. E-04 supplies the shelf the captions refer to. E-08.2 ("the biggest post is not the strongest commerce signal") is the hypothesis we verify live and E-08.5 (the silent customer) is the person we built it for. E-05.1 to E-05.4's funnel is the scale we extrapolate DM debt against. E-06.1 is the constraint: leverage, not less relationship.
concepts.handles_1600_drop: Stakeout does not survive the drop, it eats it — the concept that gets stronger at 16:00, a real strategic advantage when most teams will spend that half hour patching. Each of E-09's four findings is already an output column: 61%-no-DM is the acts-without-asking rate, the 2.4x saver multiplier is the save-probability weighting, 41%-via-private-share is the share question, and the 4.6-day median lag is the axis we add live. The one build inside the window is the LAG VIEW: re-render the funnel on a time axis so the 200 ghosts resolve across 0-14 days with the 4.6-day median marked, making the drop's central finding a visible feature rather than a footnote. New pitch line written at 16:05: "Four hours ago we were predicting engagement. We are now predicting the 61% of buyers who will never touch anything you can measure."
concepts.trust_safety: It never touches the audience, which is the cleanest safety story in this case file. No message sent, no reply automated, no follower ever interacts with software. It is a mirror Maya looks into before she speaks, so "handed to a machine" is structurally impossible. Beyond that: the ghosts are openly synthetic and traceable to the Sheet 04 personas and the E-10 rows, and we show that provenance rather than implying we surveilled real people. Outputs are probabilities with confidence, not verdicts — a 0.61 displays as 0.61 and low-confidence ghosts render faded, so it never overclaims. It generates no text: it cannot write Maya's caption, only tell her what two hundred people would do with the one she wrote, keeping authorship entirely hers. And its optimisation target is deliberately not reach — a tool that told a creator to chase views would be precisely the thing E-08.2 warns against.
concepts.build_risk: Medium, higher than Dead Drop, with a clean ladder of fallbacks. Two real risks: (a) 200 concurrent Jev requests hitting 429s mid-demo — mitigate with a Modal fan-out throttled to ~25 concurrency with exponential backoff, and cache every run so a live re-run of a caption we already tested is a replay; (b) the retrodiction not matching E-03's real ranking, which would cost the credibility beat — test this FIRST, by 13:00, because it decides whether the concept is viable, and if it fails, cut that beat and lead with the DM-debt edit. Fallback ladder: 200 ghosts live -> 60 ghosts live (still a convincing wave, ~15 seconds) -> fully precomputed for three fixed captions with the dot animation replayed from cache, visually identical and unable to fail. Build order: ghost generation and the Jev call (90 min), the grid canvas (90 min), funnel and DM-debt counter (60 min), retrodiction check (45 min), polish. Over-invest in the grid animation; it is the entire WOW.
concepts.final_line: Maya no longer needs to answer the same question 400 times because she can see, before she posts, exactly which 400 people are about to ask it — and fix it with one sentence.

concepts.name: THE FENCE — what Maya's word is actually worth
concepts.one_liner: We took one sentence Maya wrote — "Good. Not £62 good." — and turned her entire shelf into calibrated willingness-to-recommend curves, so every product has a MAYA LINE: the exact price above which her endorsement stops, which is at once a buying tool for Emily, a negotiating weapon for Maya, and a product brands would pay for.
concepts.audience_member: Emily, 22 — price sensitive (Known Associates, Sheet 04/17): "I trust you, but I am not spending £100 on serum." Needs confidence within a budget. Reinforced by E-01.4 @sarah, "is the cloud cream actually worth £38 or am i being influenced" — the exact question this answers — and E-01.11 @lucy, "what would you do if it was your money?"
concepts.decision: "Is this worth what it costs, or am I being influenced?" Not which product — whether the price is fair by Maya's standard. Every existing tool answers a cheaper-alternatives question; nobody answers the trust question, which is the one Emily is actually asking and the only one that requires Maya's judgement rather than a price-comparison API.
concepts.how_it_works: In a heist, the fence is the person who tells you what the goods are actually worth. E-04.6 is the file's one explicit contradiction and it is planted deliberately: Glass Drop, £62, Maya rating 8.1, note "Good. Not £62 good." That single sentence encodes a price threshold — she likes it, and she will not endorse it at that number. The product generalises that threshold across the shelf. For each of the ten E-04 products we sweep a price ladder (£12 to £110 in £4 steps, 25 rungs) and ask Jev at every rung whether Maya would tell her audience it is worth that money, with her two calibration anchors in the state: SPF 50 at £26, rating 9.6, "Non-negotiable" (emphatic yes) and Glass Drop at £62, rating 8.1, "Good. Not £62 good." (emphatic no despite a high rating). That is 250 NOULs, batched ~20 per request, about 13 requests, a few seconds, under a penny. Each product yields an endorsement curve, and the MAYA LINE is the price where it crosses 0.5. The findings are immediate and quotable: Glass Drop's line lands around £44 against a £62 sticker — £18 of price her audience is being asked to pay that her judgement does not cover. SPF 50's line lands ABOVE its £26 sticker, meaning she would defend it higher; that product is underpriced relative to her trust. A second, orthogonal sweep — product x budget band x skin type — asks whether she would spend THIS person's limited money on it, a different question from whether it is worth its price, and produces the audience-facing view. Three surfaces, all reading the same cached array so every interaction is instant: EMILY'S VIEW (set your budget, see the shelf ranked by worth-it gap rather than by price, Maya's line beside each sticker), MAYA'S VIEW (ten curves on one chart, her shelf priced by her own standard), and THE BRAND DESK (a brand drops in a product and a price and gets an endorsement probability plus the price at which it would clear 0.5).
concepts.jev_role: Two sweeps, both pure NOUL, both batched ~20 questions per request. Sweep 1, the price ladder: state = {product: the full E-04 row including rating and verbatim note, calibration: the SPF 50 row and the Glass Drop row with her contradiction spelled out, voice: her subject-file rule, 'willing to say what is not worth buying'}. Questions `p12`...`p110`, one NOUL per rung: instructions "Would Maya tell her audience this product is worth £X of their money?", criteria true: "She would say buy it, this is a fair price for what it does", false: "She would say it is good but not worth that — the price is doing work the product does not." 10 products x 25 rungs = 250 judgements. Sweep 2, the budget matrix: state = {product row, buyer: budget band and skin type}, question `spend` — NOUL, "This person has £Y in total for skincare. Would Maya spend it on this?", criteria true: "Yes — this is where their limited money should go", false: "No — there is a better use of a constrained budget." 10 x 5 budget bands x 4 skin types = 200 judgements. Plus one SCORE per product for the honesty badge — instructions "How would Maya characterise the gap between this product's price and its value?", criteria ["Underpriced, she would defend it higher", "Fair", "Slightly rich", "Good but not worth the money", "She would tell you not to buy it"] — 10 judgements, whose returned level text becomes the label on the card. ~460 judgements total, under a penny, generated once and cached. The front end never calls Jev; the slider interpolates the cached curve, which is why dragging a price handle updates the endorsement number at 60fps.
concepts.hero_visual: One chart, full bleed, dark. Ten thin curves sweeping top-left to bottom-right — endorsement probability against price — each in a muted product colour. Two marks per curve: a small white tick at the real sticker price, and a bright vertical MAYA LINE at the 0.5 crossing. Nine of the ten ticks sit at or left of their line. One does not. Glass Drop's £62 tick is stranded far to the right of its £44 line, in a red nothing else on the chart uses, with a dashed connector labelled +£18 and, floating beside it in her own typeface, "Good. Not £62 good." One image that makes a subjective throwaway sentence look like a measured physical quantity. Secondary shot, Emily's view: a £60 budget dial, the shelf reordering live, each card carrying its sticker, its Maya line and a plain-English badge — SPF 50: "she'd pay more than this"; Glass Drop: "good, not worth the money".
concepts.demo_90s:
30s THE TARGET — One sentence on black, huge: "Good. Not £62 good." Then: "This is the only contradiction in Maya's entire file, and it is the most valuable thing in it. She rates that serum 8.1 out of 10 and she will not tell you to buy it. Her audience asks her this constantly — @sarah: is the cloud cream actually worth £38 or am I being influenced. Nobody can answer that except Maya, because it is not a fact about the product, it is a fact about her standard. This is Emily. She trusts Maya and she is not spending £100 on serum."

90s THE HEIST — The chart builds, ten curves sweeping in. "We asked Maya's judgement the same question two hundred and fifty times, at every price from twelve pounds to a hundred and ten. That is her standard, drawn." The Maya lines drop in. Then Glass Drop's red tick lands £18 to the right of its line and the room gets it. Flip to Emily's view: set the dial to £60 and the shelf reorders — not cheapest first but best-value-by-Maya's-standard first, Red Reset and SPF 50 on top with their badges, Glass Drop at the bottom flagged "good, not worth the money", her sentence attached. Drag the dial to £30 and watch it reorder instantly. Then the third screen, and this is the one for the commercial prize: THE BRAND DESK. Type in a fictional brand's £89 serum. Endorsement 0.19. Drag the price down; at £47 it crosses 0.5. "That is Maya's rate card for her own credibility, and right now she negotiates it from memory."

60s THE SCORE — "Her superpower in her own file is one line: willing to say what is not worth buying. That is worth money to exactly three people. Emily, who stops being influenced. Maya, who can now say no to a brand with a number instead of a feeling. And the brand, who finds out before the campaign instead of after. We got all three from ten products, one contradiction and four hundred and sixty yes-or-no questions costing less than a pound." Then: "Maya — is £44 the right line on Glass Drop?" and move it live.
concepts.why_wow: It produces a measurement of something everyone assumed was unmeasurable. The room expects AI to summarise or recommend; it does not expect a chart assigning a defensible number to a creator's integrity. The moment the £18 gap appears — derived from a sentence containing no number — is a genuine intellectual surprise rather than a UI flourish, and intellectual surprise is what wins MOST INVENTIVE. It also has the rare property of being useful to three different parties on three screens inside ninety seconds, which is exactly what a commercial-potential judge is listening for.
concepts.commercial_potential: Potentially the biggest business here and certainly the most defensible, because it creates a price rather than a feature. Three revenue lines. (1) BRAND SIDE, the large one: creator-fit pricing intelligence sold to beauty brands and their agencies — "before you brief 50 creators, find out which of them can endorse this product at this price without burning trust." A real, currently unserved budget line sitting next to influencer-marketing spend, priced per campaign (£2-10k) rather than per seat. (2) CREATOR SIDE: Maya gets a negotiating instrument. Her no is currently a feeling; this makes it a number, which raises her rate and lets her decline with evidence. Bundle at £149/mo, or take a percentage of the deals it reprices. (3) MARKETPLACE, the endgame and the one Tano would care about: if every creator on the platform has calibrated endorsement curves, Tano becomes the clearing house matching brand briefs to creators who can honestly endorse at the offered price — matchmaking on integrity rather than follower count, with a take rate. The asset compounds: curves for thousands of creators across thousands of SKUs is a dataset nobody else has and which cannot be scraped, because it encodes judgement rather than behaviour. Honest risk: the brand-side buyer is a slower sale than creator SaaS.
concepts.elegance: One question, asked 250 times at different prices, produces a continuous function. That is the entire mechanism. No model to train, no elasticity regression, no pricing theory — just a yes/no question and an axis, with calibration falling out of Jev returning probabilities instead of answers. Two evidence rows do all the grounding: SPF 50 anchors the yes end, Glass Drop anchors the no end, and everything between is interpolation the model does itself. The output is a single chart a creator, a brand and a 22-year-old with £60 can all read without explanation. And as with the others, demo-time cost is zero because the curves are cached arrays.
concepts.inventiveness: This is the concept nobody in that room will have. Everyone will read E-04.6 as a cute detail; we read it as a boundary condition and reconstruct the function it implies. The inventions: treating a subjective note as a threshold rather than a label; sweeping a continuous variable through a yes/no primitive to manufacture a curve, a use of Jev that is in no cookbook; defining the MAYA LINE as a new, nameable metric (trust-adjusted price) that a judge can repeat to someone else the next day; and inverting the same cached data to serve the audience, the creator and the counterparty on three screens. It is also the only concept of the three producing an asset with value OUTSIDE the creator's own audience, which is what separates a feature from a company.
concepts.evidence_used: E-04.6 (Glass Drop, £62, 8.1, "Good. Not £62 good.") is the seed and the hero — the file's single planted contradiction, which E-08.3 explicitly flags as a discounted lead, so we are building on the sheet's own warning instead of ignoring it. E-04.5 (SPF 50, £26, 9.6, "Non-negotiable") is the opposing calibration anchor. All ten E-04 rows — price, rating, note — are the dataset. E-04.8 ("Beautiful, but too much for me", 7.7) and E-04.7 ("Boring in the best way", 8.6) give secondary calibration on taste-versus-worth. The subject file's "willing to say what is not worth buying" and pet peeve "generic automation" sit in the state as voice constraints. E-01.4 (@sarah, "actually worth £38 or am i being influenced") and E-01.11 (@lucy, "what would you do if it was your money?") are the demand evidence. Emily's persona line supplies the budget axis. E-07.2, the receipt with one item crossed out twice, is the visual motif for the refusal badge. E-07.4 ("People do not need more products. They need confidence.") is the thesis.
concepts.handles_1600_drop: This is the concept most exposed by the drop and we should say so rather than pretend otherwise — the curves are about price, E-09 is about invisible behaviour and timing. It is not damaged, but it needs a deliberate 30-minute move. The move: the drop says median lag from exposure to purchase is 4.6 days and 41% of high-value buyers arrived via a private share. Both are price-anxiety symptoms — you do not deliberate for 4.6 days about a £26 SPF you have been told is non-negotiable; you deliberate about a £62 serum whose worth you cannot verify, and the thing you forward to a friend is a second opinion on spending money. So we add a fourth surface: the SECOND OPINION CARD, a shareable object carrying one product, its sticker, its Maya line and her sentence, designed to be the thing Megan forwards to her sister. Cross-check E-10 for support: those buyers spent £38 to £122 and did it days later, exactly the band where a Maya line changes the outcome. Revised line: "The 4.6-day lag is not patience. It is an unanswered price question. We answer it in advance and we make the answer forwardable."
concepts.trust_safety: The product's entire output is a constraint on selling, which makes it the hardest of the three to mistake for automation. It generates nothing; the only prose on any screen is Maya's own note plus a label she can edit. Every curve is overridable — the Maya line is a draggable handle and moving it rewrites the shelf instantly, so her judgement always beats the model's estimate, and the demo shows that happening. It never speaks to the audience in her voice and there is no conversational surface at all. The one genuine risk is false precision: a curve implies more certainty than a sentence contains. We defuse it with visible confidence bands, an honest chart label ("estimated from Maya's own notes — she sets the line"), and a requirement that she signs off before any curve reaches the brand desk. On the brand side the ethical posture is the selling point: the tool exists to stop a creator endorsing something at a price she does not believe in, which is the opposite of what influencer-marketing software normally does.
concepts.build_risk: Low on compute, medium on making it land. ~460 judgements is trivially fast and cheap; the front end is one chart plus two panels over a cached JSON. Real risks: (a) curves coming back non-monotone or flat, which would kill the visual — test in the first 45 minutes on three products, and if noisy, fit a monotone isotonic regression through them, ten lines and honest because we plot the underlying points; (b) Glass Drop's Maya line not actually landing below £62, which would remove the hero moment — the single make-or-break check, run before 12:00, though very likely to hold given how the note is phrased and how strongly it anchors; (c) three-surface scope creeping past eight hours — build Emily's view and the curve chart first and treat the brand desk as a 45-minute stretch goal, since it is the commercial argument but not the demo's core. Fallback if the sweep is unusable: collapse to the five-level honesty SCORE per product, which still badges every card and still tells Emily what is not worth the money, just without the chart.
concepts.final_line: Maya no longer needs to argue about what a product is worth because her standard is now a number she owns — and it says no eighteen pounds before she has to.

case_strength_assessment:
HONEST VERDICT: Case 003 has the highest ceiling and the second-best floor. It is the right pick if we are optimising for BEST COMMERCIAL POTENTIAL + MOST INVENTIVE. It is the wrong pick if we are optimising for "does it work" safety.

WHY 003 WINS ON THE THINGS WE SAID WE CARE ABOUT:
1. THE ROOM IS THE AUDIENCE. Corgi Cafe, Shoreditch, ~54 builders. That room is full of Clara (wants the route in), Jamie (wants her framing on his own decision) and Noor (seed-stage offer or stay put). A verdict on "should I take the seed-stage job" lands on the judges personally in a way "which moisturiser" cannot. We can demo ON a judge. That is a decisive, unfakeable advantage and it is unique to 003.
2. COMMERCIAL POTENTIAL IS NOT CLOSE. Maya and Sofia are affiliate businesses; the ceiling is a link-in-bio with taste. Aditi is Head of New Media at a European tech title — she has a budget line, an employer, 42K newsletter, advisory revenue and keynote fees. A 003 product is B2B media infrastructure ("judgement licensing", "dark-social attribution"), not a creator toy. Tano's own pitch is "the AI creator-led growth partner" — 003 is the only case where the product is plausibly something Tano resells to enterprises.
3. UNIQUE TWO-SIDED MANDATE. 003 is the only brief that asks for BOTH a creator decision ("what to make next") AND an audience next step. That legitimately buys us two screens inside a 90-second demo without looking unfocused. 001 and 002 are audience-side only.
4. THE CREATOR WROTE OUR SPEC. E-05.3 literally says "let people bring me their own decision" and "maybe the answer is not a newsletter". E-05.5: "People want my judgement, not my calendar." No other case hands you the product statement in the creator's own handwriting.
5. LIKELY LESS CROWDED. 001 is the headline case (17 sheets, a voice note, a discounted-leads sheet, and per our notes the creator physically walks in at 17:00). Most teams will take 001. Standing out in a field of 20 skincare quizzes is harder than being the only serious tech-media entry.

THE REAL WEAKNESSES, STATED PLAINLY:
a) 003'S INVENTORY IS THE SPARSEST OF THE THREE. E-04 gives eight rows with only ASSET/TYPE/VOLUME/STATUS/"ADITI SAYS". Cases 001 and 002 give numeric creator ratings AND prices AND attributes. 003 names the useful fields (Room, Format, Decision, Cost, Aditi rating, Personal note, "Would I do it again?") but does NOT populate them. We would have to author that ledger ourselves. That is an hour of work and a genuine "use of the evidence" exposure if a judge notices we invented 53 of 61 rows. Mitigation: label synthesised rows visibly and keep the eight real ones verbatim and in the hot seats.
b) 003 HAS NO DISCOUNTED-LEADS SHEET AND NO VOICE NOTE. Case 001's E-08 and E-06 are the best anti-obvious-answer material in the pack. 003 folds a thinner version into E-05.7/E-05.8. We lose the "the case file told us not to build a DM bot" line unless we borrow it across cases (we can — it clearly applies).
c) "WHAT TO MAKE NEXT" IS INHERENTLY DASHBOARD-SHAPED, and criterion #1 is "value to a real audience member". Concept 2 below is the most beautiful and the most at risk of a judge saying "that's for her, not for me." Any 003 build must land an audience-member moment inside the first 45 seconds.
d) OUTPUT IS UNVERIFIABLE IN A WAY SKINCARE ISN'T. "Cloud Cream for dry skin" is checkable against Maya's written routing rules in two seconds. "Take the seed-stage offer" is not falsifiable on stage. We must manufacture verifiability — which is exactly why Concept 2's back-test against E-03's five real posts, and Concept 1's deliberate refusal, matter so much. Without one of those, 003 fails "does it work".
e) WE HAVE SUNK COST IN 001. Our own benchmarks doc is already validated against Maya's shelf: 100% recall on her documented rules, the £62 refusal, the Alex-saves-not-scrolls finding. That is a working, accuracy-proven pipeline. Switching to 003 throws away a head start worth maybe 90 minutes. Per our own strategy note the engine should be case-agnostic and driven by a JSON case pack — if that holds, the cost is closer to 45 minutes and we can close the demo by hot-swapping Maya in, which is a strong "this is a machine, not a one-off" beat.

RECOMMENDATION: Pick 003 IF we commit in the first hour to authoring a real ledger and to a hard verifiability beat. If we are wobbly on either, 001 is the safer win. Do not pick 002 — it is 001 with less evidence and a weaker creator story.
named_person_and_decision: NOOR (@noor.kh, E-01.2). Her DM to Aditi, still unanswered, sitting inside the 130+ from E-02's 22:15 entry: "Ok but if you were me, would you take the seed-stage offer or stay put?" The decision: leave a stable job for an early-stage company, or stay. She is not asking for information — she has all the information. She is asking someone who has been in that room to weigh it the way they would weigh it for themselves. She is the E-07.2 Jamie pattern (wants Aditi's framing applied to his own decision) and the E-09 pattern at once: she will decide roughly nine days from now, she will never click a link, and Aditi will never find out what she chose.

concepts.name: SECOND CHAIR
concepts.one_liner: Bring Aditi your own decision and get her calibrated verdict in thirty seconds — including the one fact that would change her mind, and an honest refusal when she was never in that room.
concepts.audience_member: Noor (@noor.kh, E-01.2) — "if you were me, would you take the seed-stage offer or stay put?" Secondary: Jamie (E-07.2), Tom (E-01.4, £600 budget), Rhiannon (E-01.9, build in public without annoying her employer).
concepts.decision: Take the seed-stage offer or stay in the current job — made confidently, today, without Aditi ever seeing the DM.
concepts.how_it_works: One screen. You state your decision in Aditi's own frame — the four questions she says she keeps answering (E-05.2) plus the two options, what you give up, your runway, and what you want in three years. Five fields, twenty seconds, no chat box. That input plus a compiled JUDGEMENT PACK (her rule from the subject file, her KEEP/MAYBE/KILL list, her margin notes, and every "ADITI SAYS" line from the access ledger) becomes one Jev state. One request fires roughly forty-five questions in parallel: twelve nouls, each one of her documented heuristics phrased in her own recorded words; one choice for the lean; five scores for reversibility, true cost versus stated cost, access gained, reputational risk and timing; and one gate noul — "does Aditi's access ledger contain a room that earns her the right to answer this at all?" Code, not a model, composes those atoms into a single verdict number, so the weighting is inspectable and nothing is generated. Then the inventive part: the app mutates your situation into twelve counterfactual variants (runway 6/12/24 months, equity up or down, London or Bangalore, employer constraint on or off) and fires twelve more requests concurrently — about 540 calibrated judgments, roughly 1.2 seconds, well under a cent by our measured 123-in/29-out per judgment. That sensitivity sweep tells you not just her answer but the single fact that flips it. If the gate noul fails, the product refuses in her voice and names the room she would have needed to be in. The verdict is a URL, built to be forwarded rather than clicked.
concepts.jev_role: Per decision, ONE request with ~45 questions over a shared state {aditi: {rule, keep_maybe_kill, margin_notes, ledger_notes}, asker: {...}}. Twelve nouls, one per documented heuristic, e.g. instructions "Would Aditi say this to her sister on the phone?" criteria {true: "she would say it plainly, unhedged", false: "she would soften it or change the subject"}; and "Is `asker` optimising for the room or for the work?"; and "Does `asker` already know the answer and want permission?". One choice for the lean over {take_it, stay, not_enough_information, wrong_question} — 'wrong_question' matters, it is how the product reframes rather than answers. Five scores, each four levels, over reversibility / true-cost-versus-stated / access-gained / trust-risk / timing; the float between levels drives the bar geometry, the confidence drives opacity. One gate noul over the ledger: "Has Aditi been in a room that earns her the right to answer `asker.decision`?" criteria {true: "a specific ledger entry covers it", false: "she would be speculating about a room she was not in"}. Then 12 perturbation requests x 45 = 540 judgments per run. Total for the live demo including the refusal example: ~1,100 judgments, ~2.5s wall at our measured 100-way concurrency.
concepts.hero_visual: A dark dossier card, single screen, no scroll. Top centre: one needle on a horizontal axis, STAY on the left, TAKE IT on the right, resting at 0.71 with the number set in a heavy mono face. Beneath it, a vertical stack of twelve horizontal bars growing outward from the centre line — each bar is one of Aditi's heuristics, labelled in a handwriting face with her actual words ("one true thing about a room I was actually in", "would I say it to my sister on the phone", "people want my judgement, not my calendar"). Bar length is the Jev probability; bar opacity is the confidence; direction is which way it pushes. Three bars are visibly doing most of the work and they glow. Bottom third: a strip of twelve small tiles, the sensitivity sweep — eleven are the same cool colour, one is red and reads "RUNWAY 6 MONTHS". Under the strip, one line: "This is the only thing that changes her answer." Bottom bar: ONE next step in her voice, and a single evidence chip — "IN THE ROOM: E-04.1, six founder stage interviews, 'best material I have'." Nothing else on screen.
concepts.demo_90s: 0-30s THE TARGET: "This is Noor. At 2am she sent Aditi a DM: 'if you were me, would you take the seed-stage offer or stay put?' It is still unanswered. It is one of a hundred and thirty. We did not steal Aditi's inbox. We stole her judgement." (Aditi's own line on screen behind: People want my judgement, not my calendar.) 30-120s THE HEIST: four clicks to load Noor's situation. Hit RUN. 540 judgments land in about a second and the twelve bars grow outward with her handwriting on them; the needle settles at 0.71 TAKE IT. Read the three heaviest bars aloud — every word is hers. Then grab the runway slider and drag 18 months to 6: the needle swings across the axis to STAY and one sensitivity tile goes red. "That is the only thing that changes her mind — and now Noor knows exactly what to go find out before Friday." Then paste Elena's message from the inbox, E-01.7, 'can you do a version of this for someone outside tech'. The product REFUSES: 'Aditi was not in that room. She will not answer this one — here is the one question worth actually sending her.' 120-180s THE SCORE: flip to Aditi's side. Three hundred and forty decisions arrived this week, clustered. The largest cluster, ninety-six people, is stay-or-jump at seed stage. Ninety-one per cent of them never sent a DM. "That cluster is her next video, and she did not have to read a single message to find it."
concepts.why_wow: Three things the room has never seen together. A machine that refuses to answer — in a hackathon full of products desperate to answer. A verdict that visibly FLIPS when you drag one slider, which turns an opaque recommendation into something you can interrogate. And the fact that the model never writes a single sentence: every word on that screen is Aditi's, from the evidence, and Jev only supplies the weights. That is why it cannot drift out of her voice, and it is a one-sentence answer to WOULD I TRUST IT.
concepts.commercial_potential: Three layers, ascending. (1) Direct-to-audience: Aditi's 42K newsletter at 1% conversion to a £7/month 'seat next to her' is ~£35K/year from one creator with zero additional hours — and it is revenue from the 71% who never click anything, which is revenue that currently does not exist at any price. (2) The real business: judgement licensing for expert-led media. Every trade title, every VC platform team, every accelerator, every Head of New Media has exactly one person whose judgement is the bottleneck and whose calendar cannot scale. This is a per-expert seat product, £500-2,000/month, sold into media orgs — and Aditi personally is the buyer, not just the subject. (3) For Tano specifically: the aggregate decision-cluster view is a content-planning dataset nobody else can build, because it is generated by people voluntarily stating their decision rather than by scraping behaviour. That is a data moat with consent built in.
concepts.elegance: One screen. One request. One number. No chat, no thread, no login, no generation. The entire product is: her recorded heuristics, weighted by a calibrated model, composed by twelve lines of arithmetic you could print on the card. You can explain the whole mechanism in one sentence and every element on screen traces to a specific line of evidence.
concepts.inventiveness: Nobody will build the abstention. Every team in that room will build something that answers; we ship the only product whose headline feature is knowing when Aditi has not earned the right to speak — which is her stated rule turned into executable code. Second: sensitivity-by-parallel-perturbation. Counterfactual analysis is normally prohibitively expensive; at Jev's price a full twelve-variant sweep costs a fraction of a penny, so we can show the SHAPE of her judgement rather than a point estimate. Nobody does counterfactuals in a hackathon demo. Third: the verdict is an object designed to be forwarded, not clicked.
concepts.evidence_used: E-01.2 Noor (the named person and decision), E-01.7 Elena (the refusal demo), E-01.4 Tom's £600, E-01.9 Rhiannon's employer constraint, E-01.12 Aisha 'opened this three times, still deciding'. E-05.1 KEEP/MAYBE/KILL plus the sister-on-the-phone rule, E-05.2 the four questions she keeps answering (these become the input fields verbatim), E-05.3 'let people bring me their own decision' (the literal product spec), E-05.5 'People want my judgement, not my calendar' (the tagline on screen), E-05.7/E-05.8 'how I decide, not just where I happened to be standing'. E-04.1-E-04.8, the access ledger, used as the right-to-answer index for the gate noul. Briefing 02 'one true thing about a room I was actually in'. E-02 (130+ unanswered at 22:15, the 44 useful questions). E-07.2 Jamie. E-09.2 and E-09.3 in the closing beat.
concepts.handles_1600_drop: Designed for the drop before it opens. The product's entire premise is helping someone decide WITHOUT clicking, DMing or waiting for Aditi — which is precisely E-09.1. We hold back one view and activate it live at 16:00: THE RETURNER. Because the median lag is 9.2 days and 3+ saves predicts a 3.1x action rate, the verdict is not a one-shot answer, it is a file that stays open. Come back on day four with what you found out, add it, and the panel re-runs; the screen shows your own convergence curve across returns, with the needle tightening. That directly instruments the 9.2-day window that every dashboard is blind to, and it converts 'saves' from a vanity metric into an actual product mechanic. Plus the verdict card is the forwardable unit, which is how we touch the 44% arriving by forward.
concepts.trust_safety: It never speaks as Aditi in generated prose — this is the single most important design decision. It shows her actual recorded sentences with a calibrated weight attached, so the user is reading her, not an impression of her. It cites which room earns the answer. It refuses outside her access rather than bluffing. And it always ends with 'if you want to argue with this, here is the one question actually worth sending her' — so it feeds the human relationship rather than intercepting it. Aditi said she LIKES answering people; this does not take that away, it removes the 41 duplicate 'which event was this' messages so the ones she does answer are the ones worth her time. It is not a bot, there is no conversation, and nobody is handed to a machine — they are handed a document.
concepts.build_risk: LOW-MEDIUM, the safest of the three. Core is one HTML page plus a FastAPI proxy plus a single Jev request shape we have already benchmarked (45 questions in one request measured at 0.38s for 60). The sensitivity sweep is twelve copies of the same request with a mutated field — no new code paths. The real work is writing the twelve heuristic nouls in her voice, which is a 45-minute evidence-reading job and is the same work that wins 'use of the evidence' anyway. FALLBACK LADDER: if the sweep is unstable, drop to three perturbations instead of twelve (same visual, fewer tiles). If time collapses entirely, ship verdict + refusal only — still a complete, demoable product with the best trust beat in the room. Hard cut-off: the creator-side cluster view at the end is the first thing to go.
concepts.final_line: Aditi no longer needs to be awake in six countries at once, because her judgement now answers the decision instead of the DM.

concepts.name: COLD STORAGE
concepts.one_liner: Aditi has already made the thing she should post next — it is sitting in a folder called 'unfiled'; this ranks all 61 assets by the audience decision each one actually ends, and back-tests itself against her last five real posts on stage.
concepts.audience_member: Clara / 24 (E-07.1) — wants the route in, not the story; watches six times, saves, then researches alone; LOW CLICK / HIGH ACTION. Her decision: how do I get into that room. The thing that would end it already exists, uncut, in nine hours of walk-home voice notes (E-04.4, 'where the real thinking is', status: UNFILED).
concepts.decision: Two decisions, one mechanism. For Clara: 'how do I get in' — ended by an asset that already exists. For Aditi: which of 61 things she has already paid for with her life to cut and ship this week, instead of filming more.
concepts.how_it_works: Two sides of a market. SUPPLY is the access ledger: 61 assets, with the eight from E-04 verbatim and the rest populated across exactly the fields the case file names as useful — Room, Format, Decision, Cost, Aditi rating, Personal note, 'Would I do it again?'. DEMAND is twelve recurring audience decisions distilled from the inbox and her own notes, each weighted by real volume from the field notes (41 'which event was this', 44 useful questions a day, 2.6K replies a month). Jev computes the full cross product: 61 x 12 nouls — 'does this asset END this decision, in a way Aditi would stand behind?' — plus per-asset scores for carries-judgement-versus-carries-calendar, would-she-do-it-again, was-she-in-the-room, and the sister-on-the-phone test. That is roughly 1,000 judgments, batched as ~61 requests, about two seconds by our measured throughput. Then the crucial architectural move: those atomic scores are PRECOMPUTED and the front end re-weights them in pure JavaScript, so four sliders re-rank the entire board at 60fps with zero further inference. Finally the verifiability beat: we push her five ALREADY-PUBLISHED posts from E-03 through the identical scoring, having never told the model their results, and plot predicted intent against actual sign-ups. Every row in the MAKE NEXT queue clicks through to the audience-facing card that asset becomes — the thing Clara actually receives.
concepts.jev_role: One request per asset, carrying twelve decision-nouls plus four judgement-scores = 16 questions over a shared state {aditi: {rule, keep_maybe_kill, curate_5, contradiction_note}, asset: {...}, decisions: {d1..d12}}. Noul instructions: "Does `asset` end `decisions.d4` for someone in that situation, well enough that Aditi would stand behind it?" criteria {true: "they stop researching and act", false: "they still have to ask her"}. Scores, four levels each: "Does `asset` carry Aditi's judgement or only her calendar?" (levels from 'pure access, no verdict' to 'a decision she made, with the arithmetic'); "Would she do it again?"; "Was she in this room, or reporting on it?"; "Would she say this to her sister on the phone?". 61 x 16 = 976 judgments, ~61 concurrent requests, ~2s wall. Plus the held-out back-test: 5 published posts x 16 = 80 more. Total ~1,056 judgments live on stage, well under two cents. Every subsequent slider drag is ZERO Jev calls — code re-weights the stored atoms, which is the whole reason the interaction feels instant.
concepts.hero_visual: A 61-row by 12-column grid filling the left two-thirds of a dark screen, rows labelled with asset names in mono, columns with the audience decisions in her own phrasing ('which event was this?', 'how do I get in?', 'was it worth it?', 'what would you have asked?'). The grid is mostly cold, near-black blue. A handful of cells burn. The eye is pulled straight to one row — E-04.4 WALK-HOME VOICE NOTES / 9 HRS / UNFILED — which is hot across five separate decisions, and to E-04.2 CANNES LIONS / 40 CLIPS, which is a dead cold line all the way across with the note 'everyone only saw the glamour' beside it. Right third: the MAKE NEXT queue, ranked, row one reading 'THE BACKSTAGE ANSWER → ends "was it worth it?" → 611 people waiting → 12 minutes to cut'. Across the top, a thin validation strip: five dots for her five real posts, predicted rank versus actual sign-ups, the two lines running almost parallel, with the 3.9M-view Cannes post sitting at the bottom of both. Four sliders along the bottom: REACH ←→ INTENT, EFFORT, TRUST, and one greyed out and locked.
concepts.demo_90s: 0-30s THE TARGET: "Aditi has sixty-one assets she has already paid for with four months, six countries and her actual life. Nine hours of her best thinking is in a folder literally called unfiled. Meanwhile the Cannes clips — forty of them, three point nine million views — produced sixty-two sign-ups. She does not need to make more. She needs to know which of the sixty-one ends somebody's decision." 30-120s THE HEIST: hit RUN. A thousand judgments land in about two seconds and the grid ignites. Point at the hot row: the unfiled voice notes. Then the proof — "we scored her last five published posts without telling it the results." The validation strip draws: it put the 320K-view backstage answer ABOVE the 3.9M-view Cannes post, which is exactly what actually happened, 806 sign-ups against 62. Then grab REACH ←→ INTENT and drag: the whole board re-ranks live, instantly, with no further inference. Click the number one row and it opens the card Clara receives — the route in, the cost, the one next step. 120-180s THE SCORE: "This week that is one twelve-minute cut instead of another week of filming. And at four o'clock this afternoon the case changed —" unlock the fourth slider, SAVE-WORTHINESS, and the board reorders on stage.
concepts.why_wow: An entire content strategy computed in front of the room in two seconds, and then a machine independently rediscovering the case file's own punchline — that the 320K post beat the 3.9M post — from nothing but her subjective notes. The back-test is the most powerful 'does it work' proof available in any of the three cases, because it is falsifiable against data printed in the brief that we withheld from the model. And the sliders are pure showmanship with real substance behind them: a thousand precomputed calibrated judgments re-weighting at 60fps.
concepts.commercial_potential: The clearest business of the three and the easiest to price. Aditi is Head of New Media at a European tech title — she is not a hobbyist, she has a budget line, a team of three and an employer with an archive. Every creator-led media business, every agency, every brand with a content library sits on thousands of assets and decides what to publish by vibes. Sell per-title seats at £500-2,000/month, or per-archive. Expansion is obvious: agencies with 4,000 unused assets per client, conference organisers sitting on recorded talks, B2B marketing teams with dead webinar libraries — all the same product. And it needs no integration and no tracking: it runs on an inventory spreadsheet plus the creator's own notes, so the sales cycle is a day, not a quarter. For Tano this is the analytics layer that bolts directly under a growth partnership and it produces a recurring reason to log in.
concepts.elegance: The product never generates anything. Its entire claim is 'you already made it'. One matrix, four sliders, one queue — and the moment you understand that rows are supply and columns are demand, the whole thing explains itself with no narration. The re-weighting architecture is the elegant core: judgment is expensive and atomic, arithmetic is free and composable, so you buy the judgments once and sell interactivity forever.
concepts.inventiveness: Treating a creator's archive as INVENTORY and the audience's recurring decisions as DEMAND, then clearing the market between them, is a framing nobody in that room will arrive at — everyone else will build a content-ideas generator. Two further moves nobody will make: scoring the SUBJECTIVE column as the primary signal (the case file says outright 'the subjective layer is not noise, it is the product' — so 'everyone only saw the glamour' is a feature value, not decoration), and back-testing on held-out published posts, which is an ML-evaluation instinct applied to a creator demo.
concepts.evidence_used: E-04.1 through E-04.8 in full, with the 'ADITI SAYS' column as the dominant scoring signal and the named useful fields as the schema. E-03.1 through E-03.5 in full as a HELD-OUT validation set — the five posts with their views, saves and sign-ups, withheld from the model and revealed after prediction. E-01.1 through E-01.12 collapsed into the twelve demand columns. E-02 field notes for the demand weights (41 unread, 44 useful, 9 minutes of unfiled voice notes, 130+ at 22:15, 42,000 people waiting on a newsletter draft that gets closed again). E-05.1 KEEP/MAYBE/KILL as ground truth for four assets we can check against. E-05.2 the four questions she keeps answering as the highest-weight columns. E-05.4 'STOP MAKING COURSES. CURATE 5.' — this is literally the curate-five machine. E-05.6 the contradiction, which is the product thesis: make each judgement carry more of her context. E-07.1-E-07.4 as the four audience profiles the cards are addressed to.
concepts.handles_1600_drop: This has the single best 16:00 beat of any concept in this document, because we can pre-build it and hold it visibly in reserve. From 10:30 the interface ships with a FOURTH SLIDER, greyed out and locked, labelled with a censored bar. At 16:00 the envelope opens and says the valuable behaviour is saves, forwards and a 9.2-day lag, not clicks. We unlock the slider — SAVE-WORTHINESS / FORWARD-SURVIVABILITY, driven by two extra nouls we ran at the same time as everything else ('would someone save this and come back to it in nine days?', 'does this survive arriving cold to someone who does not follow her?') — and the entire board reorders in front of the judges. We say one sentence: 'we ran these this morning and kept the column locked.' That turns the twist from a threat into our strongest proof that we read the case before the case changed.
concepts.trust_safety: It recommends only things SHE made, about rooms SHE was in. It never invents content, never writes a caption, never drafts a post. Every cell in the grid is explained by her own sentence about that asset, shown on hover. It cannot make her sound like anyone else because it does not write — it ranks. And it is explicitly the opposite of an automation product: it does not publish anything, it hands a human a shortlist and she decides. The audience-facing card it produces is her material, cut, with the decision it answers stated plainly — which is more context than a link, not less.
concepts.build_risk: MEDIUM. The dominant risk is the ledger: authoring 61 rows with credible Room/Decision/Cost/rating/note values is an hour of writing, and a judge could fairly ask which rows are real. Mitigate by keeping the eight E-04 rows verbatim and visually marked as PRIMARY, and by making the hot cells land on real rows — which they will, because E-04.4 and E-04.2 are the case file's own planted answers. Second risk is the grid render at 61x12 with hover; keep it a plain CSS grid, not a charting library. FALLBACK LADDER: drop to 24 assets x 8 decisions — still visually dense, still reads as a matrix, halves the authoring time. If the back-test is not ready, cut it and lean on the sliders; but fight for the back-test, it is the 'does it work' answer. Absolute floor: the ranked MAKE NEXT queue with no grid, which is still a product.
concepts.final_line: Aditi no longer needs to decide what to make next, because the sixty-one things she has already made now tell her which decision each one ends.

concepts.name: DEAD DROP
concepts.one_liner: Forty-four per cent of Aditi's highest-value audience arrives by forward and she has never seen a single one of them — so we replaced the shared link with a decision, addressed to whoever it was sent to, and made the chain visible without a tracking pixel.
concepts.audience_member: Ella / 26 (E-07.4) — forwards Aditi's clips into a team channel, the team acts, Aditi never sees it, LOW ATTRIBUTION. On the receiving end: Yusuf (E-01.11) — 'my manager sent me your keynote clip because he thinks I need it' — who has a thirty-two minute video and no idea what to do with it. And Meera (E-01.5), sending it to her sister 'because she is doing exactly this right now'.
concepts.decision: Ella's decision: what do I send, to whom, and why does it apply to them — right now she sends a link into a channel and it dies. Yusuf's decision, one hop later: what am I supposed to do with this, and does it apply to me at all.
concepts.how_it_works: Ella hits share on any Aditi asset and does not get a link. She gets one field, and the field asks the only question a forwarder can actually answer: who is this for? She types it the way she would say it out loud — 'my sister, she has been offered a role at a seed-stage company in Bangalore and she is scared'. That one line, plus Aditi's full access ledger, goes to Jev as a single state. A parallel burst judges every asset in the ledger against that one stranger — does this apply to them, what does acting cost them specifically, was Aditi in a room that earns this, would Aditi send this to her own sister — roughly 370 judgments in under a second and a half. What comes back is a DEAD DROP: a single card addressed to the recipient's situation, and critically it is often NOT the asset Ella picked, because Jev judges which piece of Aditi's access actually applies. The card carries two lines of reasoning in Aditi's own words, a cost sized to that person, and one next step. The recipient opens it cold, having never heard of Aditi, and gets a decision rather than content — plus a 'pass it on' button that starts the next hop. Every hop is a consented, measured event with no pixel and no last-click, because the forwarder volunteered the context. Aditi's side is a graph of everywhere her judgement actually travelled.
concepts.jev_role: One request per handoff: ~61 asset-nouls plus five recipient-scores = 66 questions over state {aditi_ledger: [...61], recipient_line: "...", forwarder_note: "..."}. Asset noul instructions: "Would Aditi send `aditi_ledger[i]` to `recipient_line`, given what she actually has to say about it?" criteria {true: "it directly ends the decision that person is in the middle of", false: "it is interesting but not their decision"}. Recipient scores, four levels: what acting actually costs this person; how far into the decision they already are; whether they need permission or information; whether this survives arriving from a stranger; whether a next step exists that they can do this week. One gate noul: "does Aditi's ledger contain a room that earns the right to advise `recipient_line`?" — same abstention discipline. Three live handoffs in the demo = ~200 judgments plus the seeded graph replay. Cheap, fast, and each handoff is visibly one request, which keeps the mechanism legible.
concepts.hero_visual: THE CHAIN. Full-bleed dark screen, a force-directed graph. One bright node at the centre labelled with Aditi's backstage answer. One edge out to a node labelled ELLA. Then three edges out of Ella into three cards laid side by side — and this is the shot: the SAME source asset has produced three visibly different cards, different lengths, different costs, different next steps, one of them a different asset entirely. Behind the cards, the rest of the graph is animating outward, a few hundred nodes propagating over a timeline scrubber marked in days, and nodes flare gold at the moment they ACT — most of them flaring somewhere around day nine, nowhere near any link. Bottom right, a hard counter in mono: NEVER CLICKED 71% · VISIBLE TO HER ANALYTICS 0 · VISIBLE HERE ALL OF IT.
concepts.demo_90s: 0-30s THE TARGET: "Forty-four per cent of Aditi's highest-value inbound arrives through a forward. She cannot see any of it. This is Ella. She forwards Aditi's clips into her team channel; the team acts on them; Aditi has never met a single one of them. Every product in this room today is built for the person who asks. We built for the person who passes it on." 30-120s THE HEIST: Ella shares. One field. She types 'for my sister — offered a seed-stage role in Bangalore, she is scared.' Three hundred and seventy judgments, under two seconds. The card comes back and it is NOT the clip Ella picked — it is the backstage answer, because that is the room Aditi was actually in for that person. Now do it twice more from the same source asset with two different recipients pulled from the inbox — Yusuf's manager and Meera's sister — and put the three cards side by side. "Same judgement. Different arithmetic. One generic answer fails all of them, and that is the whole case file on one screen." 120-180s THE SCORE: flip to Aditi's view. The chain. Scrub the nine point two days and watch nodes flare gold far away from any link. "This is the audience she has never been able to see. She did not install a tracker to see it. She just made the thing worth forwarding."
concepts.why_wow: It makes the invisible visible, which is literally the thesis of the sealed envelope, and it does it with the most viscerally impressive visual available — a propagation graph animating over time. And the three-cards-side-by-side moment is the single cleanest proof of Jev's actual superpower in the entire document: same state, same judgement, different recipient, materially different answer, computed in parallel in front of the room.
concepts.commercial_potential: The largest and most defensible business of the three, and the one a VC in the room would chase you down the stairs about. Dark social is the biggest measurement hole in the creator economy: every brand, every creator platform, every affiliate network is structurally blind to the forward, and last-click attribution gets it exactly backwards by crediting the click while the value sat in the share. A share object that carries context AND consented measurement is a category, not a feature. Revenue: per-creator SaaS for the card builder, plus a take-rate on attributed conversions that currently cannot be attributed at all, plus an enterprise tier for brands who want to know what their sponsored content did after it left the feed. It is also the most natural thing for Tano itself to own — it is the measurement layer underneath every growth partnership they sell, and it compounds, because every forward recruits the next user.
concepts.elegance: It replaces a link with a decision. That is the entire product. One field for the forwarder, one card for the recipient, one graph for the creator. No accounts, no scraping, no pixel, no consent banner — the measurement is a side effect of someone voluntarily explaining why they thought of you.
concepts.inventiveness: Highest of the three by a distance. Every other team in that room will build for the person who ASKS, because the asker is the one who shows up in the inbox. We are the only team that will have noticed that the case file's most valuable character never asks anything — and the case file explicitly tells you to notice: E-10's closing note says the link-click column is 'intentionally incomplete. You are supposed to decide what matters, then decide what to instrument.' Almost nobody will read that as an instruction. We treat it as the build order, and we instrument the forward instead of the click.
concepts.evidence_used: E-07.4 Ella (the named person). E-01.5 Meera's sister, E-01.11 Yusuf's manager, E-01.3 Sanaya adapting London to Bangalore (the adaptation case is exactly what a forwarded card has to survive). E-09.4 the 44%, E-09.2 the 71%, E-09.3 the 9.2 days, E-09.5 the 3.1x at three or more saves. E-10 in full and literally — the twelve tracked users U-014 through U-288 become the first twelve nodes of the graph with their real saves, shares, returns and days-to-act, so the animation is driven by the case file's own table, and U-241 (two saves, two shares, never acted) is visible as the honest negative. E-04, the ledger, as the candidate set for every handoff. E-05.5 'People want my judgement, not my calendar'. Briefing 03's Forwarder persona, flagged INVISIBLE.
concepts.handles_1600_drop: It IS the drop. This product cannot be built without the envelope's finding, which means the moment the room opens it at 16:00 our product is retroactively validated in front of everyone. The risk is the inverse of the usual one: we are showing our hand for five and a half hours before the reveal. That is fine and possibly an advantage — teams around us see a graph of forwards and do not know why, then at 16:00 the organiser reads out '44% arrived through a forward' and the judges remember whose screen that was. We should deliberately put the 71% / 0 / ALL OF IT counter on screen from the morning.
concepts.trust_safety: The forwarder writes the one line, not the machine — a human decided this person needed this, and the product only decides WHICH piece of Aditi applies. Nothing is scraped, no contacts are harvested, no address book is read, no pixel fires. The recipient's card opens with a human's name at the top: 'Ella sent you this.' Aditi's dashboard is aggregate and consented by construction because the data only exists when someone chose to explain themselves. In practice this is MORE intimate than a link, not less: today Yusuf gets a thirty-two-minute video and a shrug; here he gets something addressed to his actual situation by someone who knows him, with the creator's reasoning attached.
concepts.build_risk: HIGHEST of the three, and I want to be plain about it. Two views (forwarder flow and creator graph), a force-directed graph with a time scrubber, and a seeded dataset for everything beyond the twelve real E-10 rows. Graph layout eats hours and looks bad until suddenly it looks great — that is a dangerous shape at hour six. There is also a credibility exposure: the propagation beyond twelve nodes is synthetic, and if a judge asks 'is this real data' the honest answer is 'these twelve rows are from E-10, the rest is simulated' — which is defensible but is a wobble. FALLBACK LADDER, and we should decide this by 14:00: cut the graph entirely and ship the three-cards-side-by-side moment, which is the actual WOW and is maybe ninety minutes of work. Replace the graph with a static chain diagram drawn as inline SVG from the twelve real E-10 rows — no physics, no animation, all of the point. Absolute floor: one handoff, one card, one counter.
concepts.final_line: Aditi no longer needs to be in the room, because her judgement now travels to people she will never meet — and for the first time she can see where it went.
